  • This comes as, on Friday, a rare nationwide ground stop was issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration after an L3Harris router malfunction stopped the FAA's air traffic control network in its tracks, forcing thousands of aircraft to be grounded and preventing flights from departing to, from, or within the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across Newly introduced Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Dubai-based Emirates has taken a poke at the US aviation disaster that unfolded this week, posting on its social media channels that 'the skies are always open'. The original post, which included a lighthearted nod to the Microsoft Outlook and cloud outage, was then followed up with a 'was it something we remarked?'.

This comes as, on Friday, a rare nationwide ground stop was issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration after an L3Harris router malfunction stopped the FAA's air traffic control network in its tracks, forcing thousands of aircraft to be grounded and preventing flights from departing to, from, or within the US.

The post, on X, has racked up 613,000 views at the time of writing and continues to increase. The Middle Eastern airline has shared this across other social media channels, but has only reached 2,400 likes on Facebook.

Recent findings suggest that due to the four-hour delay in US flight operations, this had a ripple effect on airlines around the world, grounding US-bound services. This affected several Emirates flights, from Dubai to destinations across America. While flights already airborne were permitted to land, those still at the gate were forced to wait until final clearance was provided, and services resumed at 8:15 PM EST on Friday.

Industry observers note that emirates services were eventually able to operate to the US, with slight delays on some flights. There were no blanket cancellations or major disruptions to US-bound services. In the US, thousands of flights were canceled on Friday and Saturday, with delays expected to linger in the coming days as local airlines return to normal operations and clear the passenger backlog.

It has been revealed that experienced by airlines around the globe, flight departures were marginally delayed until clearance was given for services to resume. This had no major impact on non-UAE flight operations, and neither Emirates nor neighboring Etihad Airways or Qatar Airways saw any major displacement of aircraft or crew, unlike the thousands of canceled flights and crew timeouts experienced in the US.

Simple Flying reached out to Emirates for comment on the Microsoft Outage and ground stop; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

Sources indicate that A ground stop of this magnitude in the US has not been seen in more than a quarter century. The last time the FAA ordered a nationwide halt to all flight departures was briefly in January 2023, due to a malfunction in its Notice to Air Missions system (NOTAM). The last major ground stop was in 2001, following the September 11 terrorist attacks.

"Your email might be down, but the skies are always open" was a light-hearted jab at the Microsoft Outlook and cloud outage that disrupted millions of users of Microsoft cloud-based services and software suites worldwide. This affected Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and Copilot users.

The multi-region technical failure knocked out key collaboration and email tools for millions of customers across 74 countries. Microsoft confirmed this was not a cyber attack, security breach, or AI malfunction, but instead stemmed from a technical issue that was introduced during a network capacity upgrade. Microsoft's services were fully restored later on Thursday, but many were left in the lurch without access to these vital software systems. The global outage indirectly affected Emirates by disrupting the airline's corporate communications and internal office and email tools, while also hampering customer support channels, as confirmed by Gulf Business.

Emirates is a large international airline that operates a robust network of international flights from its home at Dubai International Airport (DXB). The airline operates a fleet of Airbus A350s, A380s, and Boeing 777s. It is the world's largest operator of the A380 and 777, and handles more than 3,600 flights per week, in excess of 500 per day, to and from the Middle East, and several unique fifth-freedom routes.

I’m on the road about half the year on assignment for TPG and on any given week, you might find me browsing the jade market in Taipei, window-shopping through Galerie Vivienne in Paris or strolling through the San Telmo market in Buenos Aires on the hunt for collectibles.

I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen a souvenir, piece of art, sweet treat or other little curio and thought, “Wouldn’t this make a great gift for so and so?”.

The only trouble is, I travel light, so there’s nary a nook or cranny in my carry-on to fit a gift, let alone several.

According to recent reports, I do, however, make a mental inventory of potential gifts I see so that I can order them for friends and family later. Here are a few of my favorite recent finds that might be perfect for someone on your holiday gift list, all inspired by my travels.

Best for: Armchair travelers who like to keep cozy.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot I love about 1 Hotels — their sustainable ethos, the Bamford bath amenities, in-room filtered water taps, the smattering of hyperlocal, destination-specific activities on offer to guests, bustling public spaces with unique dining concepts and…the bathrobes. I’m not usually a bathrobe kind of guy, but I can’t resist donning one of these ultracomfortable numbers anytime I’m a guest at one of these properties. Simple and soft, with a gray jersey-knit lining and a loose hoodie, they’re perfect for lounging with a cappuccino while you try to stave off jet lag.

TPG tip: You might want to make this purchase at an actual 1 Hotel boutique so you can earn more points per dollar with a credit card that offers a travel or hotel category bonus.

Best for: The Japanophile you want to impress.

It has been revealed that like an unstoppable force meeting an immovable object, my delight in purchasing travel souvenirs is only impeded by the limited space in my small city apartment. That’s why I love the little lacquerware boxes and trays from Zohiko, a boutique in Kyoto’s Nakagyo Ward that traces its history back to the 17th century. I especially love the finely filigreed Kirikane style, where patterns or shapes are cut out in gold or silver leaf and pressed into place. I purchased a glossy black box with gold inlay of cherry blossoms and autumn leaves on my last visit, and I keep it on my nightstand to hold my wedding ring and watch.

TPG tip: Make a trip to Japan out of it and browse the physical Zohiko boutique (you can also enjoy tax-free purchases if you’re visiting) while checking out some of Kyoto’s exciting fresh hotels.

Best for: Folks who appreciate colorful, culturally significant crafts.

Inevitably, every time I’m traipsing around Bogotá, I find myself drawn to this gorgeous little boutique in the city’s upscale Chapinero neighborhood, which sources fair-trade handcrafted pieces of art and decor from small communities around the country, including woven baskets starting at just $18. I am personally drawn to carefully carved wooden Tamo bowls from the coastal Nariño region, decorated with brightly dyed strands of wheat or barley fiber, but you can find everything from woven baskets to hammocks, jewelry and even pieces of furniture.

TPG tip: While you can often haggle for handicrafts in Colombia, prices in this boutique are as marked, so save your negotiating skills for street vendors.

Best for: Helping a friend spruce up their interior decor game.

Sources indicate that although long popular with backpackers and river cruisers, Luang Prabang still feels like an under-the-radar find in mountainous Laos, sitting on the confluence of the Mekong and Nam Khan Rivers. It’s also a hotbed of fair-trade arts and crafts. A standout atelier in town is Ock Pop Tok, an art school, store and restaurant that aims to revive, support and teach traditional Lao artistic techniques. Visitors can take classes in silk-weaving, batik-dyeing and embroidery, among other offerings. I am always tempted to buy out the textile section of the boutique, but I usually limit myself to a vibrant wall hanging or two.

TPG tip: Don’t just make a purchase; spend a few days as a student at Ock Pop Tok to pick up a newly introduced craft yourself.

Best for: Travelers who like their perfumes with a hint of historical luxury.

Of course, I’d suggest visiting the original Florence flagship of this bath and beauty purveyor, which dates back to 1221. It feels a little like visiting Ollivanders Wand Shop from “Harry Potter,” with antique cases bursting with all-natural unguents and elixirs whose formulas were originally developed by Dominican friars. But if you can’t get there, there are also locations around the U.S., including those in West Hollywood, California, Soho in New York City and Bal Harbour, Florida. I tend to keep it simple and go for the pure sweet almond oil, but you could also go regal and buy a bottle of the perfumery’s citrusy Acqua della Regina, created for Catherine de' Medici as a gift for her husband, the future king of France, back in 1533.

TPG tip: It can sometimes be less expensive to purchase these products from the original store in Florence, so why not make a trip out of it?

Best for: The fashionable cowboys at your rodeo.

Industry observers note that I love an eye-catching accessory, and belts are my statement pieces of choice. So on my last visit to Buenos Aires, I stopped by Arandu Talabarteria’s tony boutique in Recoleta. The whole store is inspired by a romanticized version of gaucho life on the pampas. You can find sturdy leather boots, billowy bombacha pants, cozy ponchos and my favorite: woven belts with intricate threadwork and high-quality leather. They start at $45 and can range into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the level of detail and craftsmanship. Best of all, you can ship to the U.S., so you don’t have to cross the equator to stock up.

TPG tip: They also have dog collars for your faithful canine companion.

Best for: The high-flying #avgeek in your life.

Recent findings suggest that if you’ve followed me for the past few years, you know I’m pretty much obsessed with KLM’s tile Delft houses, the little replicas of actual historical buildings around the Netherlands that the airline hands out to long-haul business-class passengers. I’ve attended the unveiling of each year’s new house for several years now, and my own collection has grown into a veritable village. If you have an equally #avgeeky member of your gifting circle and are looking for the perfect present, then you might want to consider buying one of these beauties for them. Historian Mark Zegeling’s “Little Kingdom by the Sea” book set, which delves into the history of all 107 of the houses, is a great accompanying gift as well.

TPG tip: Be sure to use a credit card that waives foreign transaction fees so you don’t get dinged with a 1-3% surcharge when buying your house.

Best for: Swanky sunseekers who want to make a splash.

According to recent reports, how do you tell me you summer on the French Riviera without telling me you summer on the French Riviera? You simply tote around a sunshiney yellow-and-white-striped beach bag from the iconic Carlton Cannes, the first luxury hotel to open in the city, way back in 1911. A lot has changed since then, but the simple design is meant to evoke the Côte d’Azur of yore, when you might have found Cary Grant and Grace Kelly sunbathing on the plage between scenes of “To Catch a Thief.”.

Best for: International imbibers with a sweet tooth.

According to recent reports, you might find it hard to remember your visit to Singapore, let alone pick up some souvenirs as gifts for friends, after you’ve had a few Singapore Slings at the Raffles Hotel’s iconic Long Bar. That’s why it might come in handy to pick up a keepsake Singapore Sling glass for your friends from the hotel’s online boutique. It’s like taking a sip of history with you. The nation’s signature drink was invented by Ngiam Tong Boon back in 1915 and is an intoxicating (and sweet!) mix of gin, grenadine, cherry liqueur, Benedictine, Curacao and both pineapple and lime juice. Even a sip can transport you back to a sultry Southeast Asian evening.

Best for: Your friends’ (or your own) globe-trotting tots.

We can’t forget about the kids! In my experience, there are few better or more engaging (or educational) ways to get the tykes in your life interested in travel than Little Passports, a subscription membership where each month, your child is mailed a latest box focusing on individual countries, animals, crafts and even DIY science experiments, depending on their specific subscription and age.

Best for: Your favorite skincare aficionado.

In a recent development, I first came across Officine Universelle Buly’s sweet-smelling body products during a stay at the Rosewood Hotel de Crillon in Paris last year, and I promptly swiped several tubes of shampoo, conditioner and body lotion from my suite to use at home. On my next visit to the City of Light, though, I stopped by the enchanting store in the 6th arrondissement to sniff through various scents and balms tinged with exotic notes like Madagascar amber and Maltese iris. And while you might be a Westin Heavenly Bed fan, or perhaps a devotee of DoubleTree’s signature Sweet Dreams mattress, I personally recommend a Four Seasons mattress, which has the plushest pillowtop of any hotel bed I’ve experienced. #216. Latest Update: 5 Military Aircraft Powered By Engines Found On Commercial Airliners

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

Latest Update: 5 Military Aircraft Powered By Engines Found On Commercial Airliners

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Monniaux | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying.
  • In a recent development, many military aircraft use commercially derived powerplants.
  • A Boeing spokesperson explained the benefits to Simple Flying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Monniaux | Wikimedia Commons | Simple Flying.

In a recent development, many military aircraft use commercially derived powerplants. This is especially true for transports, tankers, and maritime patrol aircraft. These uses share many engine characteristics that are also useful in commercial aviation. Examples include reliability, low maintenance costs, and fuel efficiency. It also avoids manufacturers having to spend a vast amount on engine development.

A Boeing spokesperson explained the benefits to Simple Flying.

“Using commercial-derived engines lets manufacturers and operators leverage existing design maturity, production capacity and global maintenance infrastructure. That translates into lower development risk and cost, faster fielding, more abundant spare parts and established MRO networks—while still allowing mission-specific adaptations to meet durability, fleet performance and mission capability.”.

F117 is the military designation for the Pratt & Whitney PW2000. The engine is used exclusively by the C-17 Globemaster III. The transport aircraft uses four of these engines, each rated at 40,400 lbf (180 kN). This power is enough for the aircraft to carry a payload of up to 160,600 lb (72,800 kg) with a range of 2,400 nautical miles (4,400 km). Perhaps the most impressive attribute the engine gives the Globemaster is its ability to take off fully loaded from a runway 7,600 feet (2,300 meters) long. Likewise, the aircraft can land at airfields under 3,000 feet (900 meters) long. The aircraft achieved 22 world records during its testing. Another unique feature of the engine is its thrust reversers, which can be deployed in flight, allowing it to reverse up a two-degree slope.

The F117 has gradually been improved during the Globemaster's operation and has reached a reduced-temperature configuration (RTC). This configuration uses single-crystal turbine materials that improve reliability and have lowered operating temperatures. Pratt & Whitney claims that these improvements have resulted in increased time on-wing.

Paul Gauguin Cruises has unveiled 2029 voyages exploring the South Pacific aboard the Paul Gauguin.

Fresh for 2029, a special voyage will be offered through the alliance between Smithsonian Journeys and Ponant Explorations, Paul Gauguin Cruises’ parent tech giant.

The voyage will feature the Society Islands and the Tuamotus, with onboard enrichment programming led by two Smithsonian Journeys Experts.

Guests get a $500 onboard credit that can be used for select shore excursions and activities and roundtrip airport transfers between Papeete Airport and the ship on the days of embarkation and disembarkation.

The Society Islands remain the cornerstone of the 2029 voyages through French Polynesia, allowing guests to experience the lagoons of Bora Bora and Moorea, discover Raiatea and Huahine, and explore the waters of Rangiroa and Fakarava.

Select itineraries also feature a visit to Motu Mahana, Paul Gauguin Cruises’ private islet off Taha’a.

Air traffic controller (ATC) work schedules have been scrutinized and show the reality behind the shortage of air traffic controllers in the United States. The schedule, obtained by The Washington Examiner's Anna Giaritelli, noted that controllers are scheduled to report to their facilities every single day for two weeks straight.

Sources indicate that these rosters surfaced after the standoff between controllers and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), where a 2.8% pay rise was approved but stalled by Administrator Bryan Bedford. The roster shows that the controller worked from September 20 to October 3, with the only nominal day off on a Friday, but began on a midnight shift.

According to recent reports, with 14 consecutive days on duty, the schedules indicate that the break immediately followed a Saturday night shift, beginning the evening prior at 9:00 PM. This resulted in controllers reporting every calendar day for two weeks.

In a recent development, within a single week, there is a Rattler Shift, which has controllers starting at 1:00 PM and working mandatory overtime throughout the week. Across other rosters, mandatory overtime turns a five-day standard rotation into a six-day workweek, with backwards rotating start times dropping from afternoon shifts to early mornings within a matter of days.

The shortfall of more than 3,000 controllers needed across the country highlights the deficit, with the staffing levels falling below the 85% minimum threshold at 20 of the 26 busiest airports and facilities.

Chronic understaffing results in long shifts across consecutive days. Pushing controllers to their limit. This has led fatigue rules to mandate a minimum of ten hours off between standard shifts, and 12 hours off before midnight shifts. Despite this, controllers and union leaders have warned that relentless overtime will leave too little time for individuals to rest.

In a recent development, tensions have continued to strain since the 2.8% pay rise was withheld, with controllers being told to spend at least five hours of an eight-hour shift actively working traffic positions. It has been argued that controllers should spend more time on each shift on radar or tower scopes.

National Air Traffic Controllers Association (NATCA) and controllers have pushed back, noting that the non-scope time is required for mandatory weather briefings, training, and federally mandated recuperative breaks following high-stress radar sessions. Withholding the raise after years of mandatory six-day workweeks has accelerated retirements and attrition in the agency as it struggles to rebuild the workforce.

FAA ties delayed pay to efficiency metrics that demand more on position time amid a 3,000 controller shortfall.

It has been revealed that controller staffing and fatigue can directly shape daily airline reliability and the system's resilience if a disruption hits. At understaffed facilities, an absence of just one or two workers could force the FAA to limit arrival or departure rates at major airports, like Upcoming York, Newark, Los Angeles, or Atlanta. These limitations can force ground stops or ground delay programs even on clear-weather days.

Industry observers note that the compounding strain during these outages sees the FAA already operating to its limit of staffing capacity and facing legacy systems and aging telecommunications infrastructure that is vulnerable, as highlighted by the Friday nationwide router outage that left airlines grounded across the country, displacing millions, canceling more than 10,000 flights, and leaving airline crew timed out and aircraft stranded. With a 3,000-controller shortfall and a stalled 2.8% raise, airports continue to operate at the limit of required staffing thresholds. The intense work schedules put into question how these professionals continue to work to a high standard in high-pressure environments.

It has been revealed that aging infrastructure, a long-standing deficit, federal government shutdowns, and a rigorous multi-year training pipeline show the vulnerability of the air traffic control system. The massive communications and radar failure on Friday led to the historic nationwide ground stop, which affected millions of passengers. Less than 10% of US airport control towers remain fully staffed.

#212. What Caused The FAA Meltdown? Duffy And Mullin Give Different Accounts

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15 min read (3014 words)
General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

What Caused The FAA Meltdown? Duffy And Mullin Give Different Accounts

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the most revealing moment in last night’s press conference about the FAA ground stop came when Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to explain what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy preferred to talk around: the government’s efforts the day before to update the system seem to have triggered the failure.
  • The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday evening after more than four hours of disruption.
  • I updated our original story after the press conference last night, but left it neutral, resisting the urge the opine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the most revealing moment in last night’s press conference about the FAA ground stop came when Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared to explain what Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy preferred to talk around: the government’s efforts the day before to update the system seem to have triggered the failure. That deserved a clear explanation. Instead, we got praise for President Trump, blame directed at Congress, and a demand for $50 billion.

The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday evening after more than four hours of disruption. Getting departures moving again was welcome news. Explaining why they stopped was another matter.

I updated our original story after the press conference last night, but left it neutral, resisting the urge the opine. It is worth watching below, particularly the exchanges with reporters (a full transcript is available here). But I knew I had to address the conference in a bit more depth (as One Mile At A Time has also done so well) .

Duffy described an aging communications system overwhelmed by data:.

Recent findings suggest that “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down. And — I shouldn’t say they went down; they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”.

He emphasized that the newer equipment had not failed:.

It has been revealed that “And our newly introduced IP switches did not go down; it’s the old hardware that went down. And I think the question for the American people is, do you want your Congress to fund this?”.

But what changed Friday? Old equipment does not become old overnight. What caused the overload that made a nationwide departure halt necessary?

Mullin offered a much more specific explanation:.

“What it appears to be right now is, as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment, new technology just wasn’t — it was overwhelming the older system, which is why Secretary Duffy made it very clear the patchwork doesn’t work.”.

There it is. According to Mullin’s preliminary account, the process of introducing patches and latest technology was overwhelming the older system. And look at Duffy’s reaction:.

You can see Secretary Duffy’s reaction as Secretary Mullin indicates the newer technology was overwhelming the system. pic.twitter.com/IeoW5nM4aY.

Industry observers note that those explanations are not impossible to reconcile, with the key being what Duffy left out of his explanation. Fresh equipment can remain operational while changes associated with it overload older equipment elsewhere. But that makes Duffy’s emphasis on the new switches staying online an incomplete answer to the question passengers actually needed answered and my mother always taught me that a half-truth can actually be a lie.

If the upgrade process contributed to the outage, saying the fresh equipment did not fail does not tell us whether the transition was properly managed. Later, Duffy acknowledged the limits of what officials knew:.

“So, we’re still working on the details of what went wrong today.”.

Industry observers note that “I’ll be happy to give you more information when we have it, I don’t want to give you the wrong information. Our team is working overtime trying to navigate what happened here, what was the cause and how do we prevent it in the future should similar situations arise?”.

That is a perfectly reasonable thing to say during an unfolding investigation. It would have been a much better starting point than presenting the outage as an obvious demonstration that Congress needed to send more money.

According to recent reports, I am quite certain that replacing decades-old aviation infrastructure is not easy and I expect hiccups along the way as we update our aging air traffic control systems. At the same time, I expect the people responsible for the project to explain a major failure candidly.

Something like: “The government is replacing a sprawling, aging system while keeping aircraft moving and old and new technology must coexist during the transition, but we are investigating whether a change produced unexpected consequences, and working around the clock to keep it from happening again.”.

I would have been far more understanding of that explanation.

According to recent reports, “Growing pains” cannot become a blanket defense for shutting down air traffic across the country if there is evidence of poorly tested updates, inadequate safeguards, or a failure to provide a workable rollback. But it would acknowledge the difficulty honestly. We can distinguish a hard project that encounters a serious setback from officials trying to sell that setback as proof of their own excellent leadership.

Early in the briefing, Mullin offered this assessment:.

According to recent reports, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like by the organization and the team he’s put together. We’re built to handle crises like this, and that’s exactly what we’re doing. We’re moving at an unprecedented pace as a whole of government to make sure that we are doing the public justice by making sure everybody is safe, which everybody is.”.

I am thankful passengers were safe. Halting departures when communications become unreliable is the correct decision and even with this administration I have no fear that the skies are unsafe, at least when it comes to air traffic control.

But why was a nationwide operational failure the moment to congratulate the president and his team?

#211. Tech Report: United CEO 100% Sure A Merger With American Would Get Approved. I’m 99% Sure He’s Wrong.

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words)
Business & Policy 🌐 Onemileatatime

Tech Report: United CEO 100% Sure A Merger With American Would Get Approved. I’m 99% Sure He’s Wrong.

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ll admit that there’s probably collectively a little too much reporting on what United CEO Scott Kirby indicates.
  • In April 2026, news broke about how United CEO Scott Kirby reportedly approached the Trump administration about the concept of merging with American, and forming a “flag” carrier for the United States.
  • Days later, American management publicly rejected this concept, which caused Kirby to publicly make his case for a merger with American.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ll admit that there’s probably collectively a little too much reporting on what United CEO Scott Kirby indicates. The concern is, he’s a really bright guy, and I’d argue he’s the most impactful leader in the US airline industry since Richard Anderson at Delta. At the same time, on some level that seems to have gotten to his head, and I just feel like he’s making claims that are completely indefensible, at least if you approach them with any level of objectivity.

In April 2026, news broke about how United CEO Scott Kirby reportedly approached the Trump administration about the concept of merging with American, and forming a “flag” carrier for the United States.

Days later, American management publicly rejected this concept, which caused Kirby to publicly make his case for a merger with American. Months later, it came out that Kirby had also approached Delta about the concept of a merger. Ever since, Kirby has continued to insist that this is a great idea, and that those who oppose it are just misunderstanding his vision.

The widespread belief (among other industry executives and the public) is that such a deal wouldn’t get approval, because it shouldn’t… it would be really bad for competition! However, View from the Wing flags Kirby’s latest comments on his merger dream, which I can’t help but find to be interesting:.

In a recent development, “I think the biggest impediment is having a willing partner. I am more convinced today than I was when I wrote my note six months ago that it could get approval. It could get approval because it is good for customers. So many people look at that kind of a merger through what has been the traditional airline commodity lens, that air travel is a commodity, and it doesn’t matter which airline flies. But customers care about the service, the product, the technology, the reliability. It wouldn’t be easy. We’d have to do some divestitures, but I 100% think it could get approved.”.

According to recent reports, so Kirby claims he’s 100% certain that a merger between two of the three biggest US carriers would get approved by regulators. No, he’s not 80% sure, or 90% sure, or 99% sure. He’s 100% sure. Now, in fairness to him, he acknowledges that some divestitures would be required, but I think he’s underestimating the scale of divestitures that would be required for anything like this to get approval.

Recent findings suggest that maybe this is a hot take, but I think American management should call United’s bluff. Come to a deal that’s good for American shareholders, and create an absolutely massive breakup fee in the event it doesn’t get approval. There would only be upside for American, and then Kirby can put his money where his mouth is.

We know that Kirby has an axe to grind with American, since he was fired there, and then went on to work at United (which probably ended up being the best thing that could happen to him, because he sure seized that opportunity). So I can’t help but feel like a large motivation for his merger dream is based on wanting to get revenge, and that’s maybe clouding reality for him a bit.

Fundamentally, I disagree with Kirby’s merger dream on two levels — he overstates United’s greatness, and he understates the competitive implications of a merger of this scale.

Sources indicate that united has absolutely improved massively under Kirby’s leadership. But Kirby acts like United is Singapore Airlines, while Delta and American are Air Algerie and TAAG Angola Airlines, by comparison.

It has been revealed that is Kirby forgetting that United is still catching up with Delta, and in the number two spot in the US industry? He acts as if the only way to have a pleasant flight on a US carrier is to fly with United, which just seems extreme. He seems to believe that, though, since he has called United “the best airline in the history of aviation.”.

Industry observers note that for that matter, from a consumer perspective, does Kirby not realize that the positive changes at United are now forcing American to make positive changes? American is getting seat back TVs, Starlink Wi-Fi, improved lounges, etc. That strong competition helps consumers, and it doesn’t hurt them.

Obviously eliminating one of the “massive three” carriers would have huge implications for competition, and pricing power for airlines (especially when airline executives keep talking about how they want fare increases to stick around even after fuel prices decrease).

In a recent development, kirby’s emphasis has long been on how it’s not just about offering the best price, but also about offering the best overall experience and value. While there has definitely been some decommoditization of airfare (in other words, more people are brand loyal), that still represents the minority of consumers. United is a publicly traded manufacturer that’s there to maximize shareholder value, and you can bet the airline will charge the highest fares it possibly can — if they didn’t, Kirby should be fired, because he’s not doing his job.

Recent findings suggest that even if you were to claim that domestic competition would be preserved (it wouldn’t be, in my opinion), what about internationally? The way global aviation has evolved is that the “big three” US carriers have helped create “big three” joint ventures, where they all partner with different airlines across the Atlantic and Pacific, allowing them to coordinate fares, schedules, etc. Abandoning an entire set of joint ventures would horribly hurt the competitive landscape.

United CEO Scott Kirby has for months been talking about how great it would be if United and American could merge, and he talks about how positive it would be for consumers. The glitch is that such a deal would be unlikely to get regulatory approval, given the competitive implications.

Kirby disagrees, and he’s 100% certain that such a deal would get approval. I couldn’t disagree with him more, because the competitive implications would be massive (and negative). I kind of wish American would call his bluff and agree to a merger with a huge breakup fee, so that Kirby can be forced to actually stand behind his claims.

What do you make of Kirby’s merger “guarantees?”.

#209. Industry News: How To Tell Different Airplanes Apart, From 737s To A380s: An AvGeek’s Guide

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16 min read (3106 words)
General 🌐 Onemileatatime

Industry News: How To Tell Different Airplanes Apart, From 737s To A380s: An AvGeek’s Guide

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read | Source: Onemileatatime

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The miles & points world has all kinds of different enthusiasts — some people are only interested in miles & points in order to save money on travel, while others are interested in miles & points because they love airplanes.
  • In this post, I’d like to share how I easily identify planes in a split second.
  • To keep things simple, I’ll just stick to the most popular mainline, commercial aircraft, and I’ll be talking about each “family” of aircraft in a particular section.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The miles & points world has all kinds of different enthusiasts — some people are only interested in miles & points in order to save money on travel, while others are interested in miles & points because they love airplanes. I know there are plenty of people who are very frequent flyers but can barely tell the difference between an Airbus A380 and Boeing 747.

In this post, I’d like to share how I easily identify planes in a split second. Of course there are lots of methods for doing this, but I’ll share my techniques (and maybe other hardcore avgeeks can chime in with their methods in the comments section).

To keep things simple, I’ll just stick to the most popular mainline, commercial aircraft, and I’ll be talking about each “family” of aircraft in a particular section. Let’s start with Boeing aircraft, and then we’ll cover Airbus aircraft.

Sources indicate that the Boeing 737 is the most common commercial aircraft in service. To me, there are a couple most obvious signs that a plane is a 737, as opposed to an A220 or A320.

Industry observers note that one method is to look at the cockpit windows. The 737 has six cockpit windows (which is standard), and the window at the far end on each side “slopes up” at the bottom, so the window doesn’t go as far down as on other jets. Furthermore, when you look at the tail of the 737, you’ll see that it connects with the rest of the plane with an extended slope, much more so than on the A220 or A320 (below you can see a 737 in the front and an A321 in the back).

What can make identifying the 737 challenging is that there are so many different variants. Let’s differentiate between the 737 NG (the older version of the jet), and the 737 MAX (the newer and more controversial version of the jet).

There are three most obvious ways to tell if you’re traveling on a 737 MAX. The 737 MAX has the zig-zag pattern at the back of the engines, which I’ll talk more about below, as you’ll also find this on 787s and 747-8s.

Recent findings suggest that furthermore, the 737 MAX has the split winglet, which is large going both up and down, and the edges remain flat and straight. While some 737 NGs have split scimitar winglets, the upper and lower edges of the winglet are sloped.

Lastly, the 737 MAX has perfectly round engines, while the 737 NG engines flatten out a bit at the bottom, or look more oval.

Sources indicate that how can you tell the difference between the variants? In terms of fuselage design, there’s the 737-700, 737-800/737 MAX 8, and 737-900/737 MAX 9 (with the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10 entering service soon). The 737-700 is the smallest variant, and the easiest way to identify it is based on the single exit on each side over the wing.

It has been revealed that the 737-800 and 737 MAX 8 have two exits over the wing on each side, in addition to the exits at the front and back of the aircraft. The only exception would be the 737 MAX 8200, which is operated by some ultra low cost carriers, where there’s an extra exit in the back, with nine windows behind it.

Then the 737-900 and 737 MAX 9 have two exits over the wing, plus they have an additional door plug (as opposed to an actual exit) between the wing and rear exit, which is why the window spacing is a little weird in the back.

Sources indicate that while Boeing’s modern narrow body aircraft is the 737, there are still a fair number of 757s flying around. The 757 is sort of like a flying pencil, as it’s quite long and the fuselage is narrow.

Unlike most other narrow body planes, the 757 has 10 wheels, as it has two wheels in the front, and two sets of four wheels in the back, which differentiates it from the 737, A320, etc., as those planes typically only have six wheels. The 757 also has a “proper” exit door behind the forward section, plus two overwing exits.

There are two variants of the 757 — the 757-200 and 757-300. The way to tell them apart is easy. The 757-200 does not typically have an additional exit between the overwing exits and the rear door.

Meanwhile the 757-300 does have another full exit in the rear section, with roughly a dozen windows on each side between it and the rear door. The 757-300 looks so long that you’d think it would break in half (don’t worry, it won’t).

As far as I’m concerned, the Boeing 747 will always be the queen of the skies. While the Airbus A380 has overtaken it in terms of size and passenger comfort, it can’t compete with the 747’s curves. The 747 has a full lower deck and then a partial upper deck, making it easy to identify.

While the passenger version of the 747 is becoming increasingly rare nowadays, there are two types that are most common — the 747-400 and the 747-8 (and no, it’s not the 747-800).

According to recent reports, how can you tell the difference between the two planes? For one, the 747-400 has traditional winglets that stick “up.” On top of that, the 747-400 has a smaller upper deck. Behind the upper deck exit row, there are only seven windows on each side.

As a point of comparison, the 747-8’s wingtips gradually go up, and the upper deck is bigger, with 15 windows on each side behind the upper deck exit row.

The rear of the 747-8’s engines are also similar to those of the 787, with a zig-zag pattern, as I’ll explain below.

From a distance, it’s not unreasonable to think that a 767 and 777 look alike. I even sometimes make that mistake. It’s especially tricky since there’s the 767-300 and 767-400, and they’re roughly proportional to the 777-200 and 777-300 in terms of their dimensions.

According to recent reports, what makes identifying the 767 especially tough is that many airlines have “modified” them. Some airlines have winglets on the 767, while others don’t. Some airlines have two doors on each side of the 767-300, while others have three doors.

So let me make this simple — at the base of each wing, the 767 has two sets of two wheels. In other words, on each side there are four wheels, for a total of 10 wheels on the plane (including the two nose wheels). Meanwhile the 777 has three sets of two wheels at the base of each wing, for a total of six wheels on each side. I know this might sound minor, but I’ve actually found it to be a very easy way to tell the planes apart.

How can you tell the difference between the 767-300 and 767-400? The 767-300 has at most three sets of doors on each side (and sometimes just two), while the 767-400 has four sets of doors on each side.

For me there are four identifying characteristics of the 777 — two huge engines, no winglets, a total of 14 wheels (two in the front, and six in the back on each side, with three rows of wheels there), and a vertically flat and boxy tail cone below the tail (as opposed to a rounded one on most other jets).

But how do you tell the difference between a Boeing 777-200 and a Boeing 777-300?

A Boeing 777-200 has just four doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

Meanwhile the 777-300 has five doors on each side of the aircraft (one in the very front, one in front of the wing, one immediately above the wing, one behind the wing, and one in the very back).

The easiest way to identify the 787 is by the zig-zag “cut outs” in the back of the engine, known as chevrons (designed for noise reduction). Also, the wings have a unique shape. While there aren’t abrupt winglets, the wings “stretch” pretty high up.

If you’re staring right at the front of the plane, there’s another easy identifier. The 787 is the only wide body jet to have four cockpit windows, rather than six.

How do you tell the difference between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10? Personally I can eyeball it pretty easily, but it can be tough for some people to do, since all versions of the plane have four exits on each side, similar wings, the same number of wheels, etc.

Recent findings suggest that the only real difference between the planes is the length — the 787-8 is 186 feet long, the 787-9 is 206 feet long, and the 787-10 is 224 feet long. That’s a pretty significant difference, as the longest version is over 20% longer than the shortest version.

I think a 787-8 is pretty easy to spot, because it looks quite small from the outside. Usually I look at the number of windows between the first and second set of doors. If there are 10 or fewer windows on each side (including ones that are “blacked out”), it’s a 787-8.

Meanwhile if there are more than 10 but fewer than 15 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors, it’s the 787-9.

If there are more than 15 windows between the first and second set of doors on each side, it’s the 787-10.

Industry observers note that the Airbus A220 is one of the most pleasant narrow body aircraft to fly. This is a fairly small, sleek, and modern looking aircraft. I know this might sound silly, but to me, it looks like an Airbus A350 that shrunk.

There are a few easiest ways to tell this apart from other jets. For one, unlike the 737 and A320, the A220 has four cockpit windows, rather than six. You’ll also notice that the nose of the aircraft is straighter and longer, compared to the more rounded nose of the A320.

According to recent reports, the plane also has distinctive winglets, at least among narrow body planes. The winglets exclusively go up, and are pretty straight. They’re not as curved or vertical as on the A320.

Industry observers note that there are two variants of the A220 — the A220-100 and A220-300. If you ask me, the easiest way to tell them apart is by how many windows there are between the forward door and the emergency exit over the wing. The A220-100 has roughly 12 windows on each side in this area, while the A220-300 has roughly 17 windows on each side in this area. You can also usually just eyeball it — the A220-300 looks a lot more stretched.

It has been revealed that much like with the 737, there are lots of A320 variants. There’s the A320ceo (the older version of the jet) and the A320neo (the more modern version of the jet, with “neo” standing for “latest engine option”). Then you also have several variants, including the A319, A320, and A321.

Let’s start with the difference between the A320ceo and A320neo, which largely comes down to the engines, as you might have guessed based on the “neo” name. Not only does the A320neo have bigger engines than the A320ceo, but the A320neo also has extensions at the rear of the engine at the top and bottom. In simple words, you’ll notice how the engine looks more “open” in the back, unlike on the A320ceo, where it looks like it “closes” more.

According to recent reports, now let’s talk about how to tell the variants apart. The A319 is smaller than the A320 and A321, and an easy identifier is that it typically has only one exit over the wing on each side.

Meanwhile the A320ceo and A320neo have two exits on each side over the wing, but no other exits between the forward and rear doors.

Lastly, the A321ceo and A321neo are the largest variants of the jet, and just generally look stretched. These planes have an extra set of exits, beyond the forward and rear doors, plus the two exits on each side over the wing. So you’ll either notice an extra door, or some weird window spacing toward the back of the plane. The A321LR and A321XLR are just variants of the A321neo, and from the outside, there’s not an obvious way to tell them apart.

The major challenge with identifying the A330 is that there are two very different types of these planes — there’s the A330-200/300, which is the original version of the plane, and then there’s the A330-800/900neo, which is the new version of the plane. To some people, the A330-900neo may look more like an A350-900 than an A330-300.

Let’s start with the A330-200/300. This plane is pretty “proportional” looking, and can easily be identified by the fact that it has two engines and the most “traditional” winglets out there. The winglets are an easy way to differentiate it from the other twin-engine wide bodies out there. Furthermore, the plane has four doors on each side.

The A330-800/900neo has a similar body style, except the winglets are different. While the A330-200/300 winglets are wide and point almost straight up, the A330-800/900neo winglets get narrower, and curve a bit more.

Sources indicate that the A330neo and A350 have similar general designs, though there is a big difference in the wingtips, as you’ll see below when I cover the A350. If anyone has any other easy ways to spot the difference between the two planes, please let me know.

It has been revealed that the A340 is a single deck plane with four engines, which makes it pretty easy to identify, since it’s the only non-double decker that has four engines. But how do you tell the difference between the A340-200/300 and A340-600? Okay, truth be told there aren’t a lot of these planes flying anymore, so there aren’t many situations where you’ll have to do that. With Lufthansa having just retired the A340-600, you’ll barely find the plane outside of Iran nowadays. But still….

The A340-200/300 has engines that looks disproportionately small (like, are these things gonna propel us through the sky at 500 miles per hour, or dry my hair?), and also has just four doors on each side of the aircraft.

Meanwhile the A340-600 is a gorgeous, beastly work of art. It’s so long, so skinny, and has appropriately sized-looking engines. There are also five doors on each side of the aircraft. Personally after the 747, I find the A340-600 to be the most beautiful plane. However, like I said, you won’t find it in the skies of most countries anymore.

The Airbus A350 has two main identifying characteristics — an extremely sleek design (especially near the nose, and with the Batman-looking cockpit windows), and very “steep” winglets (they’re not gradual, unlike the 787).

How do you tell the difference between the A350-900 and A350-1000? There are two main differences.

Industry observers note that for one, the A350-900 has 10 wheels, while the A350-1000 has 14 wheels. The difference comes from the base of each wing having six wheels (three rows of two) rather than four wheels (two rows of two). That’s because the A350-1000 is the stretched version of the A350-900.

It has been revealed that the easiest other way to tell the difference is based on the number of windows between doors one and two. The A350-900 has somewhere around 15 windows on each side between the first two sets of doors.

Meanwhile the A350-1000 has over 20 windows on each side between the first and second set of doors.

I don’t think anyone has trouble identifying this whale-jet, given that it has two full decks.

According to recent reports, understandably not everyone can spot the difference between airplanes, because, well, to most people it doesn’t actually matter. That being said, for us avgeeks it’s often a favorite pastime. Hopefully the above is a simple guide that can help people tell apart planes, should they be interested in learning a bit more.

While there are lots of other differences, I figure it makes sense to highlight some of the most “obvious” tricks, as opposed to studying each plane in great detail.

To fellow avgeeks, I’d be curious to hear how you easily tell planes apart!

Latest Update: Taking My Kids To Germany Turned Into Three Transatlantic Round Trips And A Detour Through Greenland

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to my next trip report, which will recount my comings and going to Europe over the summer…three round trips as it turned out.
  • I realize I will certainly not win an accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language.
  • That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to my next trip report, which will recount my comings and going to Europe over the summer…three round trips as it turned out.

I realize I will certainly not win an accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language. They are German citizens too after all. And so what I did this summer, as I did last summer and as I will do next summer, was take them over to Germany in mid-July and pick them up in mid-August.

That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.

I booked a round-trip economy class ticket in spring to get us home from our ski trip and then back in the summer, which included SWISS economy class ticket from Zurich – Chicago and Austrian economy class from Los Angeles – Zurich via Vienna and was even able to squeeze in an overnight in Vienna at the Park Hyatt, which I booked for 25,000 Hyatt points.

It has been revealed that the week I booked (the last week in February) was the week the conflict in Iran broke out and I was very happy I booked when I did because I got the tickets for $764 r/t. I also booked before United cut off awarding mileage on basic economy tickets. Since I booked on United ticketing stock, I received PQPs (status points) and RDMs (redeemable miles) for these flights. I also figured the lack of advance seat assignments would not matter because I was traveling with two young children. That gamble paid off well and we were seated together at check-in on each flight.

That got us to Germany, but I had to find a way back to the USA and then back to Europe the following month to pick them up, plus a ticket home for all three of us.

Industry observers note that flyingBlue came through with a perfectly-timed last minute 60K redemption on Air France from Basel – Paris – New York, plus €453 in taxes. It was such a pleasure to fly on Air France and I look forward to sharing all the details from my A350-900 business class flight.

Recall I landed in JFK around 10:00 pm and drove overnight to Pittsburgh, which itself was a journey. Then from there I flew home via Lisbon, Frankfurt, and Washington, DC…as one does.

It has been revealed that but then I had to get from Southern California back to Basel and decided to fly via San Francisco, Denver, Newark, Nuuk (Greenland), and Copenhagen. That was three tickets, including:.

Industry observers note that I found SAS Business Class saver award space to get the three of us back to the USA, which has to be one of the best deals out there at 60K EuroBonus miles for me and only 30K miles for the kids, which included business class from ZRH-CPH as well. Taxes were €214.59 total for the three of us.

The flight availability forced an overnight in Copenhagen, but a late arrival so we used 36,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to stay at the AC Hotel Bella Sky Copenhagen near the airport, a towering property that was perfect for the overnight layover.

I won’t review the JetBlue A220 flight to Burbank since we all fell asleep right away after too much Taco Bell in Times Square….

These are the segments for this trip report:.

I look forward to sharing this report with you!

#207. Why Airlines Schedule Flights To Take Longer Than They Used To—Even Though It Costs Them More

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20 min read (4059 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

Why Airlines Schedule Flights To Take Longer Than They Used To—Even Though It Costs Them More

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost indicates his flight to Washington’s National Airport still takes about 50 minutes, but the published schedule has grown to an hour and 42 minutes.
  • It has been revealed that he’s right that the schedule determines whether a flight counts as on time.
  • Industry observers note that my flight to DCA takes about 50 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that former Ohio Attorney General Dave Yost indicates his flight to Washington’s National Airport still takes about 50 minutes, but the published schedule has grown to an hour and 42 minutes. He thinks he’s figured out why: airlines get to look more on-time by giving themselves longer to arrive. He’s right that the schedule determines whether a flight counts as on time. But airlines pay for those extra minutes, and they generally have good reasons to avoid adding more than they need. My flight to DCA takes about 50 minutes. It used to be listed as an hour & change. The *posted* flight duration keeps getting longer, now 1hr 42 min. Still takes 50 minutes. I can only conclude that these posted durations are used in determining on-time statistics. — Dave Yost (@DaveYostOH) November 12, 2026 The Schedule Includes Time On The Ground Airlines publish block time: the time scheduled from leaving the departure gate to reaching the arrival gate. That includes taxiing, waiting for a runway, flying, and getting to a gate at the other end. And National airport is a particularly odd place to dismiss congestion. In a January update, the Federal Aviation Administration explained that it had reduced the airport’s hourly arrival rate from 36 to 26 after the January 2025 collision, before increasing it to 30. The airport could handle more – if the air traffic control system hadn’t had such challenges. More demand concentrated into busy periods, limited runway and gate capacity, controller shortages and equipment problems all affect how long the trip takes. The problem also isn’t just the average. It’s how much travel time varies. An airline needs a schedule that works when there’s a normal amount of congestion, not just when the plane gets straight to the runway and encounters no delay at the other end. If that variability grows, the schedule can need more time even when the flight takes 50 minutes in the air. I made this point when covering claims about increased schedule padding in 2023. Airport and air traffic control bottlenecks make trip time less predictable. Airlines build that uncertainty into their schedules. Airlines Pay For Those Extra Minutes I’ve been pushing back on the simple ‘they’re juking the stats’ explanation since at least 2015. Making flights look longer is an expensive way to improve a scorecard. Crew costs. Scheduled time can determine pay even when a flight arrives early. American Airlines flight attendants, for instance, receive flight time pay based on the greater of scheduled or actual block time for each flight. Less productive airplanes. Add time across the day’s flying and there’s less room for another revenue flight. The airline can wind up needing more airplanes and crews to operate the same service. Less attractive itineraries. Longer trips can lose bookings to faster connections, competing airlines, or driving. Airlines want to sell you a convenient schedule. Back in 2015, I cited Southwest Airlines’ estimate that adding just a couple of minutes of block time across its schedule would cost the equivalent of 8 to 10 airplanes’ daily flying. You can’t just push flights later in the day, because airlines need to schedule flights when people want to fly. And airlines help create some of their own congestion through banked schedules at hubs. Packing flights into connecting waves makes more itineraries possible, but it also puts more demand on gates, runways and employees at the same time. Longer Schedules Can Improve More Than The Statistics The government counts an arrival as on time when the plane reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after its scheduled arrival. But if an airline keeps missing its arrival times by small margins, increasing block time can be a sensible first step toward fixing reliability. It’s acknowledging how long operating the flight actually takes, including the delays that occur often enough to blueprint for. American confirmed longer block times alongside a redesign of their Dallas operation, moving from 9 large connecting waves to 13 smaller ones in April. I explained why that investment could pay for itself through fewer missed connections, delayed bags and disrupted aircraft and crews. In April, American’s Dallas hub chief reported that missed connections were down 50%. At United Airlines’ 2019 media day, an executive explained that 25% of their flights were expected to arrive 10 minutes early. That gave them room to hold some departures for connecting passengers and still arrive on time through their ConnectionSaver program. United had started improving its reliability with longer block times. Arriving Early Can Create A Gate Problem Of course, extra time in the schedule doesn’t create extra gates. Get in early and the gate assigned to your flight may still have another airplane on it. An empty gate may belong to another airline, be unsuitable for your aircraft, or lack the employees needed to bring you in and operate the jetbridge. I covered Doug Parker explaining this problem in 2018: American used essentially all its hub gate capacity at peak times, and a few airplanes failing to leave could leave arriving flights with nowhere to go. So you can land early, sit waiting, and reach the terminal around the originally scheduled time. The government’s arrival clock keeps running until gate arrival. Regardless, it’s not all a conspiracy to juke the stats. Often it’s just a realistic expectation for how long the airline thinks on average it’ll take to travel, though sometimes they beat those expectations. The real solution isn’t just tightening schedules, it’s improving throughput – more capacity in air travel control and at airports. In a recent development, more demand concentrated into busy periods, limited runway and gate capacity, controller shortages and equipment problems all affect how long the trip takes. An airline needs a schedule that works when there’s a normal amount of congestion, not just when the plane gets straight to the runway and encounters no delay at the other end. If that variability grows, the schedule can need more time even when the flight takes 50 minutes in the air.

According to recent reports, I made this point when covering claims about increased schedule padding in 2023. Airport and air traffic control bottlenecks make trip time less predictable. Airlines build that uncertainty into their schedules.

It has been revealed that I’ve been pushing back on the simple ‘they’re juking the stats’ explanation since at least 2015. Making flights look longer is an expensive way to improve a scorecard. Crew costs. Scheduled time can determine pay even when a flight arrives early. American Airlines flight attendants, for instance, receive flight time pay based on the greater of scheduled or actual block time for each flight. Less productive airplanes. Add time across the day’s flying and there’s less room for another revenue flight. The airline can wind up needing more airplanes and crews to operate the same service. Less attractive itineraries. Longer trips can lose bookings to faster connections, competing airlines, or driving. Airlines want to sell you a convenient schedule. Back in 2015, I cited Southwest Airlines’ estimate that adding just a couple of minutes of block time across its schedule would cost the equivalent of 8 to 10 airplanes’ daily flying. You can’t just push flights later in the day, because airlines need to schedule flights when people want to fly. And airlines help create some of their own congestion through banked schedules at hubs. Packing flights into connecting waves makes more itineraries possible, but it also puts more demand on gates, runways and employees at the same time. Longer Schedules Can Improve More Than The Statistics The government counts an arrival as on time when the plane reaches the gate less than 15 minutes after its scheduled arrival. But if an airline keeps missing its arrival times by small margins, increasing block time can be a sensible first step toward fixing reliability. It’s acknowledging how long operating the flight actually takes, including the delays that occur often enough to plan for. American announced longer block times alongside a redesign of their Dallas operation, moving from 9 large connecting waves to 13 smaller ones in April. I explained why that investment could pay for itself through fewer missed connections, delayed bags and disrupted aircraft and crews. In April, American’s Dallas hub chief reported that missed connections were down 50%. At United Airlines’ 2019 media day, an executive explained that 25% of their flights were expected to arrive 10 minutes early. That gave them room to hold some departures for connecting passengers and still arrive on time through their ConnectionSaver program. United had started improving its reliability with longer block times. Arriving Early Can Create A Gate Problem Of course, extra time in the schedule doesn’t create extra gates. Get in early and the gate assigned to your flight may still have another airplane on it. An empty gate may belong to another airline, be unsuitable for your aircraft, or lack the employees needed to bring you in and operate the jetbridge. I covered Doug Parker explaining this problem in 2018: American used essentially all its hub gate capacity at peak times, and a few airplanes failing to leave could leave arriving flights with nowhere to go. So you can land early, sit waiting, and reach the terminal around the originally scheduled time. The government’s arrival clock keeps running until gate arrival. Regardless, it’s not all a conspiracy to juke the stats. Often it’s just a realistic expectation for how long the airline thinks on average it’ll take to travel, though sometimes they beat those expectations. The real solution isn’t just tightening schedules, it’s improving throughput – more capacity in air travel control and at airports. #206. Tech Report: Forget Polaris. This United Airlines Passenger Hit The “Poorlaris” Jackpot In Economy

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words)
General 🌐 Liveandletsfly

Tech Report: Forget Polaris. This United Airlines Passenger Hit The “Poorlaris” Jackpot In Economy

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Liveandletsfly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, there are upgrades you pay for, upgrades you earn, and then there is the upgrade that requires neither money nor status: discovering that nobody else is sitting in your row.
  • A passenger shared this account on Reddit after flying from Newark (EWR) to Paris (CDG):.
  • “Won the Poorlaris lottery for EWR-CDG last night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, there are upgrades you pay for, upgrades you earn, and then there is the upgrade that requires neither money nor status: discovering that nobody else is sitting in your row. One United Airlines passenger recently enjoyed that particular pleasure on a flight to Paris, calling it a win in the “Poorlaris” lottery. I love that name.

A passenger shared this account on Reddit after flying from Newark (EWR) to Paris (CDG):.

“Won the Poorlaris lottery for EWR-CDG last night. Polaris and premium were full but the rest was empty. Felt great and well-rested!”.

“Poorlaris,” of course, is a clever name for economy class alternative to United Polaris business class: enough empty seats to stretch out and sleep. No lounge access or fancy bedding required. Just a boarding door that closes before someone appears to claim the seat next to you (and perhaps a bit of work to ensure the seats next to you stay empty, as I’ll address below).

It has been revealed that for all the attention we give premium cabins, an empty row in economy class can fundamentally transform an overnight flight. If your objective is to get some sleep before landing in Europe, being able to stretch out is more valuable than a better meal or a wider seat that still leaves you sleeping upright.

I spend plenty of time writing about business class, and I certainly appreciate a proper bed. But I also appreciate getting somewhere comfortably without spending the extra money or miles…unfortunately, I don’t rack up an endless supply of them.

It has been revealed that there is a certain satisfaction in looking toward the front of the aircraft, knowing those cabins are full, while you have room to spread out in the back. You bought the cheaper ticket and somehow ended up with something the people in premium economy cannot do: the ability to lie down.

Industry observers note that given a choice between one premium economy seat and an entire usable row in economy on an overnight flight, I would take the row. The ability to sleep matters more to me than a nicer tray of food.

It has been revealed that on my recent delayed American Airlines flight from Chicago to Los Angeles, I received a last-minute first class upgrade after many passengers abandoned the flight. I appreciated the upgrade, but even then wondered whether three economy seats would have been better. Probably!

Sources indicate that there are limits, though. Your height matters, as does the seat design. Armrests that do not move can spoil the whole arrangement so be weary of bulkhead or certain exit row seats. An economy row is still an economy row, with gaps and hard surfaces that a real business class bed does not have.

But when it works, it can work remarkably well. The operative word is “lottery.”.

A seat map with lots of unassigned seats does not guarantee an empty flight. Passengers may receive assignments at check-in or at the gate or there may be a lot of employee standbys. And an empty seat beside you during boarding may not remain empty.

I would never pay a substantial premium for a particular economy seat simply because the surrounding seats appeared unoccupied…but once boarding is complete and the crew permits you to spread out, enjoy it. Sometimes the best part of a flight is the thing you could not book in advance. If it happens, it happens.

This passenger’s account is a pleasant reminder that a great flight does not always require a premium cabin. Sometimes it just requires a few seats nobody else bought.

I still love Premium Plus, but I would happily accept a winning ticket in the Poorlaris lottery too.

On an overnight flight, would you choose premium economy or a guaranteed empty row in economy?

According to recent reports, hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there, thanks to the strong perks that they offer. In this post, I’d like to specifically focus on credit cards that offer hotel elite status, and talk about under what circumstances they could be worth it.

Sources indicate that I’ve already written about the best hotel credit cards offering free nights, either as an annual benefit or as a reward for reaching certain spending thresholds. Nowadays it’s possible to earn elite status with most major hotel group through credit cards, so let’s talk about the options there are, and under what circumstances this is actually worth it.

Recent findings suggest that I’d like to take a look at all the ways that you can use US-issued credit cards to earn elite status with a hotel loyalty program. In some cases, you get status just for having a card, and in other cases, a certain amount of spending is required.

Recent findings suggest that there are potentially all kinds of benefits to hotel elite status, ranging from free breakfast to late check-out to bonus points to suite upgrades. Obviously the higher your status, the better the perks.

In a recent development, here are all the options, going in alphabetical order based on the name of the loyalty program. Note that I’m only including credit cards that are only open to fresh cardmembers.

According to recent reports, if you’re going to stay with a certain hotel group, it goes without saying that having some elite status is better than not having elite status. At the same time, I don’t want to overpromise, and suggest that being an elite member is going to get you the most amazing treatment on earth.

After all, if you get elite status just for having a credit card, you can assume that you’re not alone in pursuing this strategy. 😉 That being mentioned, there are definitely some credit card elite status opportunities that are more lucrative than others.

In a recent development, my single favorite hotel credit card for elite status is the Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card (learn more), as it offers Diamond status in the Hilton Honors program. This gets you 100% bonus points, room upgrades subject to availability, breakfast (or a food & beverage credit in the US), lounge access at select brands, etc.

According to recent reports, as is common with the major hotel groups, the further from the United States you get, the better the elite treatment, and the better the shot of a good upgrade. Hilton Honors is my third preferred hotel group, and the Diamond status on the card does the trick for me. Given all the card’s other perks, I also find it really easy to justify.

Industry observers note that my second favorite hotel credit card is the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), as it offers Platinum status in the Marriott Bonvoy program. Don’t expect all that much when it comes to upgrades (at least in major markets), but the guaranteed perks, like late check-out, breakfast at most brands, etc., really do add up.

Sources indicate that beyond that, I think there should be a special mention for all the cards offering Hilton Gold status, given how easy it is to earn. It’s pretty remarkable that nowadays you can earn valuable status with Hilton, Marriott, and Wyndham, just for having a credit card (without a spending requirement), and with Hyatt and IHG you can earn valuable status with credit card spending.

On top of that, there are many mid-range credit cards that offer status just for having the card, which can be valuable as well. For example, it’s really easy to earn Hilton Gold elite status, and that gets you perks like free breakfast at most brands, bonus points, and more.
