#204. How The Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8, & 787 Dreamliner's Engines Create Problems No Other Modern Jet Faces

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10 min read (1925 words)
General 🌐 Simpleflying

How The Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8, & 787 Dreamliner's Engines Create Problems No Other Modern Jet Faces

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Modern commercial jet engines are among the most refined pieces of engineering ever developed.
  • It has been revealed that the distinctive sawtooth patterns visible on the rear edges of the engine nacelles were designed primarily to reduce noise.
  • Chevrons are serrated trailing edges built into the rear section of an engine nozzle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modern commercial jet engines are among the most refined pieces of engineering ever developed. They are quieter, more fuel-efficient, and dramatically cleaner than the engines that powered earlier generations of airliners. Yet three of Boeing’s most vital aircraft families, the Boeing 737 MAX, 747-8, and 787 Dreamliner, carry an unusual design feature that introduces a problem almost no competing modern jet faces: serrated engine exhaust nozzles known as chevrons.

It has been revealed that the distinctive sawtooth patterns visible on the rear edges of the engine nacelles were designed primarily to reduce noise. Boeing developed the concept alongside General Electric and NASA as airlines faced increasingly strict airport noise regulations and growing community pressure around major hubs. The system succeeded in making aircraft quieter during takeoff and landing, particularly on the Dreamliner. However, the solution came with a trade-off. The same aerodynamic mixing effect that lowers noise also creates drag and slightly reduces engine thrust during all phases of flight, including cruise, where noise reduction provides little operational benefit. Over time, Boeing itself began searching for alternatives, eventually abandoning chevrons entirely. The result is a fascinating engineering story about how one innovation solved a regulatory challenge while simultaneously creating a performance penalty that no other major aircraft manufacturer chose to accept.

Chevrons are serrated trailing edges built into the rear section of an engine nozzle. Instead of a smooth circular exhaust outlet, the nozzle edge features a repeating sawtooth pattern extending into the exhaust flow. Boeing introduced the technology commercially on the 787 before expanding it to the 747-8 and the 737 MAX family. Every 787 engine variant uses chevrons, regardless of whether the aircraft is powered by Rolls-Royce Trent 1000s or General Electric GEnx engines. The 747-8 and all 737 MAX variants also feature this design.

The engineering principle behind chevrons is relatively straightforward. Modern turbofan engines produce two separate exhaust flows: a hot, high-velocity core stream from the combustion section and a cooler bypass airflow generated by the fan. The interaction between these two flows creates turbulence, which is a major source of jet engine noise. Chevrons reduce that turbulence by generating controlled vortices that mix the exhaust streams together more gradually. The smoother transition lowers the acoustic intensity of the exhaust plume, particularly during high thrust operations such as takeoff and initial climb. NASA research conducted during the technology’s development confirmed measurable reductions in perceived engine noise around airports.

The concept emerged during a period when airport noise regulations were becoming increasingly restrictive worldwide. Airlines operating large fleets at densely populated urban airports faced growing pressure to reduce community noise exposure. Boeing saw chevrons as a way to improve compliance without fundamentally redesigning engine architecture. Visually, the feature also became associated with Boeing’s next-generation aircraft branding. The scalloped nacelle edges gave the 787 a distinctive appearance that emphasized technological innovation and acoustic refinement. For many passengers, the chevrons became symbolic of quieter modern air travel. Yet the aerodynamic realities behind the design created complications that became increasingly apparent over time.

Sources indicate that the central problem with chevrons is that the vortices they intentionally create do not simply disappear once the aircraft leaves the airport environment. The aerodynamic mixing process continues throughout the entire flight, including cruise conditions where noise reduction is far less important. Those vortices slightly disrupt the exhaust flow and increase drag, which reduces overall engine efficiency and marginally lowers thrust output. Aviation analyst Petter Hörnfeldt, better known through Mentour Pilot, has estimated that the thrust penalty from chevrons is approximately 0.5%. While that figure appears small, aviation economics are built around extremely thin performance margins where even fractional efficiency losses matter significantly.

For high-utilization aircraft such as the 737 MAX, the effect becomes cumulative. Narrowbody airliners often perform multiple short-haul sectors daily, so a minor efficiency penalty applied continuously across thousands of annual flights translates into meaningful fuel burn increases over the lifespan of the aircraft. This creates the core engineering contradiction behind chevrons. The system addresses a problem most critical during takeoff and landing, but imposes its aerodynamic penalty continuously. Unlike deployable aerodynamic devices that activate only when needed, chevrons are fixed structures permanently protruding into the exhaust stream.

The concern becomes especially relevant during cruise flight. At high altitude, engines operate in carefully optimized conditions designed to minimize drag and maximize fuel efficiency. Any disruption to exhaust flow can slightly degrade propulsion efficiency. Airlines closely monitor these performance margins because fuel remains one of the largest operating expenses in commercial aviation. The penalty also affects thrust generation. While passengers would never perceive a half percent reduction in performance directly, aircraft manufacturers compete intensely over efficiency metrics. Modern airliner programs are often marketed around fuel burn improvements measured in single digit percentages. In that context, a permanent efficiency loss becomes strategically vital. As noise regulations evolved and engine technology improved independently, the industry began exploring whether chevrons were still the best solution available.

Engine chevrons have become a defining feature of modern aircraft, but do they really pose a problem for performance?

Sources indicate that one of the most revealing aspects of the story is that Airbus never adopted the technology on any of its competing modern aircraft programs. The European manufacturer chose an entirely different path for noise reduction, relying instead on nacelle acoustic treatments, advanced fan designs, and high bypass ratio engines. Initially, Boeing’s patented chevron design prevented competitors from using the concept commercially. That patent protection remained in place until 2021.

It has been revealed that however, even after the patent expired, Airbus still showed no interest in integrating chevrons into aircraft such as the Airbus A350 or Airbus A320neo family. The firm’s reasoning was unusually direct. A350 Chief Engineer Dougie Hunter publicly explained that Airbus found no compelling advantage in the technology. According to Hunter, Airbus engineers determined that chevrons did not provide sufficient noise benefits to justify the associated specific fuel consumption penalty.

Recent findings suggest that that statement highlights an notable philosophical difference between Boeing and Airbus during the development of next-generation aircraft. Boeing embraced a visible mechanical solution to tackle airport noise. Airbus instead prioritized improvements inside the nacelle and engine architecture itself, reducing noise without altering external exhaust geometry.

High-bypass turbofan engines already produce significantly less noise than older designs because more thrust comes from slower-moving bypass airflow rather than the high-velocity exhaust core. Airbus engineers concluded they could meet regulatory requirements without introducing additional drag-inducing structures into the exhaust stream.

The divergence also reflects how aircraft manufacturers balance competing priorities differently. Boeing accepted a measurable efficiency compromise to secure stronger community noise performance. Airbus decided the operational costs outweighed the acoustic gains. Over time, Boeing itself appeared to move closer to Airbus’ position.

The clearest evidence that Boeing recognized the limitations of chevrons emerged during the development of the Boeing 777X and its GE9X engines. Despite the feature appearing prominently on the 787, 747-8, and 737 MAX, Boeing abandoned chevrons entirely for its newest flagship widebody. Instead, Boeing and General Electric developed a radically different nozzle architecture using ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs. These advanced materials tolerate extremely high temperatures while remaining substantially lighter than traditional metallic structures. Their thermal resistance allowed engineers to create a more compact and aerodynamically efficient mixed exhaust nozzle without relying on serrated trailing edges.

According to recent reports, the result achieved a similar acoustic performance while reducing drag and weight simultaneously. GE9X Chief Project Engineer Terry Beezhold explained that the fresh nozzle technology provides equivalent cabin and community noise levels but with lower drag and lighter construction. The GE9X nozzle system is reportedly around 20% lighter than older designs. This transition is significant because it effectively acknowledges the trade-offs associated with chevrons. If the technology represented the optimal long-term solution, Boeing likely would have retained it on the 777X. Instead, the firm invested heavily in eliminating the feature while preserving its acoustic benefits.

It has been revealed that the move also illustrates broader trends in engine development. Modern aerospace engineering increasingly favors integrated aerodynamic efficiency over external add-on solutions. Advanced materials, computational fluid dynamics, and improved nacelle shaping now allow manufacturers to address noise problems more elegantly than was possible when chevrons first emerged. In many ways, the 777X represents Boeing’s attempt to solve the same challenge without inheriting the same penalties.

Discover why the Boeing 777X depends entirely on the GE9X, the world’s largest and most advanced commercial jet engine ever built.

According to recent reports, despite their drawbacks, chevrons were not necessarily a mistake, particularly on the Dreamliner. Boeing found a secondary advantage that partially offset the performance penalty and made the overall trade-off more acceptable for that aircraft specifically.

It has been revealed that because the engines were substantially quieter externally, Boeing was able to reduce the amount of sound insulation material installed throughout the fuselage. Reports indicate the company eliminated up to 600 pounds, or roughly 272 kilograms, of acoustic insulation compared with what otherwise might have been required. That weight reduction improved fuel efficiency and helped compensate for the thrust and drag penalties created by the chevrons themselves. On a long-range aircraft such as the 787, where weight savings compound significantly across intercontinental missions, the trade-off became economically viable.

Industry observers note that the Dreamliner’s broader design philosophy also supported the decision. Boeing engineered the aircraft around aggressive efficiency goals using composite materials, advanced aerodynamics, and next-generation engines. The chevrons fit within that larger optimization strategy, even if they were not an aerodynamically perfect solution in isolation. The equation was less favorable on smaller aircraft such as the 737 MAX. Narrowbody jets generally lack the same opportunities for large-scale insulation weight savings, while their high cycle utilization amplifies fuel burn penalties over time. This partly explains why criticism surrounding chevrons became more pronounced as the technology spread across Boeing’s lineup.

Industry observers note that still, the system undeniably succeeded in one notable area: noise reduction. Airports and communities benefited from quieter operations, and airlines operating at noise-sensitive hubs gained regulatory and operational advantages. The problem was never that chevrons failed technically. The matter was that they solved one problem while creating another.

According to recent reports, boeing’s use of engine chevrons on the 737 MAX, 747-8, and 787 Dreamliner represents one of the more unusual engineering compromises in modern commercial aviation. Developed alongside NASA and General Electric to reduce airport noise, the serrated nozzle design successfully lowered acoustic output by improving exhaust flow mixing.

In a recent development, yet the same vortices responsible for quieter operations also introduced drag and reduced engine efficiency throughout every phase of flight. That trade-off created a challenge virtually unique among major modern airliners because Airbus rejected the concept entirely, preferring alternative acoustic technologies that avoided continuous performance penalties. Boeing itself eventually moved away from chevrons on the 777X, replacing them with a more advanced low-drag nozzle architecture built around ceramic matrix composites.

The story illustrates how aviation engineering rarely produces perfect solutions. Every design decision involves balancing competing priorities, including noise, fuel efficiency, weight, emissions, maintenance, and regulatory compliance. Chevrons solved a real operational problem during a critical period in commercial aviation development. But over time, advances in engine and materials technology revealed that quieter aircraft did not necessarily require permanent aerodynamic compromises.

#203. American Airlines Reverses Its Original Newly introduced York Strategy—Wants Local Customers Back In Major Cities

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 35 min read (6990 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

American Airlines Reverses Its Original Newly introduced York Strategy—Wants Local Customers Back In Major Cities

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 35 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • American Airlines states focusing on local customers has produced “material margin improvement” at LaGuardia.
  • Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too.
  • That’s a full rejection of the Latest York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American Airlines states focusing on local customers has produced “material margin improvement” at LaGuardia. They’re doing better in New York by focusing on the needs of New Yorkers. Meanwhile, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said at at Thursday’s Skift Aviation Forum that he sees Chicago’s biggest opportunity in winning corporate traffic, and he’s working on Los Angeles schedules that better serve the people who live there too. That’s a full rejection of the New York strategy American laid out in 2014, immediately after the US Airways merger. They wanted to bring passengers to New York, rather than offer a schedule for New Yorkers. That was dumb. They thought they couldn’t compete in New York, and they walked away from the credit card spending of New Yorkers. American Chose Not To Be The Airline For New Yorkers The original post-merger strategy was building schedules around people coming to New York for business and then going home. Arriving in the morning and leaving in the evening works for an out of town visitor. A New Yorker making a day trip wants the reverse. American dropped LaGuardia service to Cleveland, Minneapolis and Atlanta while adding cities like Roanoke and Wilmington, North Carolina. They were using scarce New York slots to strengthen their appeal to customers they believed were underserved elsewhere in the country, instead of building a schedule to take people who lived in New York to the places they needed to go. It was an extension of the old US Airways playbook of avoiding direct competition. By 2018, Robert Isom was pitching a boutique business airline for New York, built around London, premium transcons and a limited collection of other routes. That was already a change from the original inbound strategy. It still missed that the person buying a business class ticket to London also takes their family on vacation. And by not providing either a better product or a more well-rounded schedule, they were setting themselves up to be a ‘spill carrier’ taking business only when offering a lower price that competitors wouldn’t meet. The JetBlue partnership demonstrated what a broader network could do. In October 2021, I reported American’s fastest growing markets for AAdvantage signups were its JetBlue and Alaska partnership cities. Doug Parker Explained The Credit Card Math Problem In March, I wrote about former American CEO Doug Parker’s explanation of how airlines allocate credit card revenue to routes. He described assigning the money to flights where customers redeem their miles. That accounts for the seats being used. It doesn’t tell you which flights caused the customer to get the card and put spending on it in the first place. A New Yorker might use their miles for Hawaii. But they chose American because it worked for their trips to Chicago, London and Miami. If American stops being useful for those trips, the customer may switch airlines and cards. Crediting the Hawaii flight doesn’t capture what the New York schedule was doing for the business. That was my criticism of American’s retreat seven and eight years ago: cutting a flight can improve its route accounting while making the company worse off by losing the customer’s other business. You can’t count the card revenue twice, but you need to count what disappears when the customer leaves. Chicago And Los Angeles Need The Same Rethink This is also why the O’Hare fight matters beyond departure counts and Scott Kirby’s desire to beat American. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months. As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May said their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects. Meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s plans to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier: I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the significant markets in the world In his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the plan was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30. American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation. American has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens. So 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will! The Alaska Partnership Fits This, Too American nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. At the employee meeting I covered in January, Pieper reported 20% growth in Chicago loyalty enrollments and 20% growth in card acquisitions over the preceding nine months.

As I explained when Chief Financial Officer Devon May addressed Chicago profitability in March, allocated overhead, network effects and credit card economics can produce very different answers to whether a hub makes money. May remarked their usual flight profitability systems don’t directly capture all those card effects.

In a recent development, meanwhile, American withdrew Los Angeles long haul flying and became less useful to local customers. In October I contrasted the old network strategy with Pieper’s aims to reverse it. He’d told Brett Snyder at Cranky Flier:.

I fundamentally believe we need to fly our own airplanes to the big markets in the world.

Industry observers note that in his Skift comments, he describes schedule changes continuing through 2027 toward a 2028 terminal rebuild and a 30-gate operation. Yet in his October 12 interview with Cranky Flier, the strategy was 25 gates across terminals 4 and 5, while Pieper wanted all 30.

American’s fifth lease amendment, approved by the City Council on December 10, 2025, provides for 25 preferential use gates after Terminal 5 reopens: all 15 in Terminal 4 and 10 in Terminal 5. LAWA’s 30-gate description is for the entire two-terminal complex, not American’s allocation.

Recent findings suggest that american has been using 5 Tom Bradley terminal gates, but those are temporary replacements during Terminal 5 construction. American can seek additional Bradley, but they aren’t assured five permanent extras. The lease also ends LAWA’s obligation to accommodate American at the remote Eagle’s Nest when the rebuilt Terminal 5 opens.

Recent findings suggest that so 25 is the documented allocation in terminals 4 and 5, and 30 is the larger operation Pieper wants. It’s not clear to me how he’s able to say that they’ll have them – I hope they will!

Recent findings suggest that american nearly threw away its Alaska partnership for a related reason. As I reported when Parker explained the reversal in February 2020, American had seen Alaska’s purchase of Virgin America as creating more route overlap, turning a partner into a competitor. But Alaska had strength in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest that American lacked. Those customers could make American’s flights more valuable, and a broader combined offering could win corporate accounts neither carrier could serve as well alone. The original plan had American operating long haul flights from Seattle, supported by Alaska. Bangalore and Shanghai never started. London started and then disappeared. Alaska bought Hawaiian and began building the international airline American hadn’t delivered. As I wrote in September, bringing Alaska into the Atlantic joint venture with British Airways and partners, and the Pacific venture with Japan Airlines, would change the incentives. American would have a financial interest in selling Alaska’s international flights, while the foreign partners could bring customers from the other end. They could coordinate schedules rather than merely put a codeshare on an existing flight. More Flights Aren’t Enough To Win Scott Kirby was explaining the network and credit card connection back in 2017. United needed better domestic schedules to win customers, who would then become prospects for its card. American needs to repair the parts of its network that prevent it from earning a customer’s broader business. But I also pushed back on Kirby’s assumption that network size would win the card business. The competition includes bank cards with transferable points and cash back, not just another airline’s card. American’s newer Citi relationship makes the network and product investments more consequential. As I wrote last month about its ambition to approach $10 billion in annual loyalty partner payments, acquiring a cardmember, keeping them, and getting them to spend are different tasks. That’s why it matters tremendously that American is working to build a better airline. And it matters that they preserve the quality and advantages of their AAdvantage program. Without either of those, the gambit gets expensive fast but doesn’t deliver the hoped-for results. Sources indicate that I’m not surprised to hear AA talking about wanting to be more competitive in Upcoming York, Chicago, and Los Angeles. They’ve been running a promo, seemingly targeted at travelers who have flown American for business, offering bonus miles for segments to/from/through NYC/ORD/LAX.

According to recent reports, AA is finally starting to learn the lesson that George Costanza learned. Every instinct that they have had for the past 10 years has been wrong. So, just do the opposite.

You really do have to wonder how much longer Devon May can survive. He’s been on the wrong side of every product decision at AA and been the key voice against product improvement.

But it’s also a very AA phenomenon — keeping bad leaders who have never shown a shred of strategic thinking.

Sources indicate that speaking from the position of a +40 year ~4 million-mile Platinum Pro A/Advantage customer, when American began abandoning Latest York for both transcontinental and international flights, I began abandoning American and it will take a lot to bring me and many other top tier former loyal NYC area customers back. Unfortunately, the airline has been mismanaged and mistreated loyal customers since Bob Crandell left in 1998 and both shareholders and loyal customers have suffered. It’s time for a major overall of both senior management and the Board and a new attitude/approach from American’s current poor customer service team.

Day by day Nat and Heather are fixing the Vasu, Parker and Isom effups.

They can reshuffle the existing fleet to serve both segments…early morning locals departing the hub and early morning visitors to the hub.

It has been revealed that this is good to see and it is reflected in the schedules (for example, JFK-ORD is now 4 x daily) and the resumption of JFK-SEA with 2 x daily (which will be complemented by the AS flying). AA has some holes to fill in its NY portfolio. It should fly from JFK to SAT for example, and continue to pick up markets that B6 is walking away from. Eventually, American will have the majority of the B6 portfolio to themselves and that will unlock their ability to be a competitive force in the NYC market. AA must still continue to refine and improve its offering and maintain and grow the pivot to premium. The money is in the NYC, Chicago, and LA markets, not in the sunbelt.

Industry observers note that @Gary–This article is an excellent analysis. I agree that flight times are notable to local passengers. When I visit NYC or Chicago, I like to depart such that I arrive in the mid to late afternoon. That allows me to check into a hotel upon arrival and have the evening to get a good meal, go to a show, erc. I like to come home on a late afternoon flight ti maximize my time on the trip. (That kind of scheduling appeals to leisure travelers as well as business travelers.). If I lived in NY or Chicago, I would like similar schedules if flying west.

@Joe–I agree that whenever possible, an airline should try to schedule in a way that works for both ends of the city pair.

It has been revealed that @Peter – exactly right! Best post of the day.

Industry observers note that I would add AA needs to add back a few non stop flights from NY and BOS to South Florida and Orlando. This is the key to winning the NY/ BOS domestic market.

Seems like Parker and Kerr (the US Airways CFO who served at AA until 2023, promoting May) were the ones who are most responsible for where we are now – finance ran the show. Vasu, and even Isom inherited a lot of the implications of their thinking.

And let’s not forget Kirby before he learned new ways at United – decisions in the early 2010s set up the fleet and network we have today.

Industry observers note that southwest has a miniscule presence in New York. Delta has a miniscule presence in Chicago. Yet both are much more profitable than American. How can that be?

Industry observers note that @DesertGhost – Delta has #1 at JFK/LGA and #1 at LAX. They themselves say the reason for AUS expansion is card revenue. Southwest is huge in California. Huge in Florida. And has lower costs. And their profits aren’t that much higher than American’s.

According to recent reports, AA should also try to add SAN, maybe CPH and ZRH from JFK. Also should build more of a focus city at Boston Logan. There is card revenue there!

Is it possible AA could get from ~11% of JFK market share to 15-20%?

this is precisely why Scott Kirby is paranoid.

AA is coming back and UA can no longer count on revenue that AA has been bleeding for years.

It has been revealed that DL’s focus on “stealing from” AA was largely pre-covid and at LAX during covid. DL is comfortable w/ its domestic size now and is not focused on market share and is reaping the profits accordingly even while continuing to take share from B6 in the NE.

AA is the largest domestic airline because of their size in a whole lot of small and medium sized cities.

AA steal carries a lot of low fare traffic it should not be carrying but it cannot get rid of it until it replaces it with higher quality revenue in coastal cities.

I opened up my iPhone camera to guide me, but I could barely see what I was doing since the plane lights were off. You can imagine my surprise—and envy—when my best friend, Deanna, illuminated our row with her travel makeup mirror. It seemingly came out nowhere, and was already propped up on her seat tray, showing her exactly where she needed a touch-up. “I'm gonna need to borrow that,” I stated.

Sources indicate that the pre-flight touch-up was not the only time Deanna's travel makeup mirror came in handy on our trip. One night before dinner, as 12 girls simultaneously got ready, she and I realized we were running short on bathroom mirrors. Rather than wait for the bathroom to clear and be forced to rush, or be late, we took turns doing our makeup with her travel mirror. Before we landed back at Newark Airport after the trip, I had already ordered Funtouch's travel makeup mirror for myself on Amazon.

Commerce editor Meaghan Kenny is using the Funtouch travel makeup mirror in the car.

Industry observers note that after a few months of having my own, I can honestly say this $17 travel accessory is worth every penny. While I initially envisioned using it on the plane or a crowded girls trip, it's proven handy on numerous occasions. Most recently, on a trip to Newport, Rhode Island, I pulled out my foldable travel mirror and did my makeup en-route. It was a relief to arrive at The Vanderbilt hotel looking and feeling put together, without having to sit through the whole four-hour car ride with a full face of makeup on first thing in the morning.

It has been revealed that it's very simple to use: Unfold the mirror to reveal its full size, then tap the touch-screen button in the center to turn on the light. It offers three different light settings, including white light (my favorite), warm light, and cool light. The same button turns the light off too. And if that's a little too much light, say on an early morning flight, you can long press the touch-screen button to dim the brightness level. Another perk: The mirror stands up on its own, so you don't have to worry about holding it or propping it up against anything.

The travel makeup mirror has three different light settings to choose from.

Sources indicate that I love that the device is wireless. It comes with a USB charger so I can make sure it's powered up before I travel with it and leave the cord at home. The battery life is pretty impressive—I didn't need to recharge it after my four-day trip to Rhode Island. The portable device is also very slim—about the size of a Kindle or an iPad Mini—so it can be slipped into a tote bag, backpack, or weekender bag with ease. Its exterior is pretty durable too, so I don't need to worry about it getting crushed in my bag.

Another thing I appreciate about this travel makeup mirror: no magnification—I don't need to see my pores that close! The mirror is just the right size to show you your full face, head, and neck without being bulky or heavy to travel with. It's lightweight, compact, and portable—the trifecta of any good travel accessory. If you're stumped on what to get someone you love this season, surprise them with something they'll actually use every time they travel. You might want to grab one for yourself too.

In a recent development, earlier this year, a friend gifted me this two-sided compact mirror from Chanel. Not only is it super sleek, but it's small enough to fit in my tiniest purses. I never leave the house for a date night or girls dinner without it. It's the perfect size for me to swiftly pull out to touch up my lip liner in an Uber or at a restaurant. It's a practical yet glamorous stocking stuffer for the friend who's always on the go.

According to recent reports, this Amazon find earns major points for its versatility. The foldable mirror with LED lights can be rotated, and its stand can be adjusted to different heights. There's also a spot at the base of the mirror's stand that can hold your phone, so you can follow a makeup tutorial or watch a movie while you get ready.

It has been revealed that this travel makeup mirror looks pretty similar to mine, but it has a few extra bells and whistles. For starters, it features a adjustable stand that can be rotated back and forth to give you the best angle. It also has a smart sensing system, meaning the mirror lights up automatically when you open it, and turns off when the device is closed. If you, unlike me, do enjoy seeing your pores up close, this option comes with a small, detachable magnifying mirror.

It has been revealed that another foldable travel mirror, this one features a row of LED lights and a touch-screen button that can be used to adjust the brightness level. This compact mirror is smaller than iPhone, making it a smart choice for smaller bags or those just in case moments.

Industry observers note that smaller than a credit card and cheaper than an iced coffee, this $4 compact mirror is just the right size to slip into a purse or crossbody bag. Consider it your secret weapon to check if you have anything stuck in your teeth after dinner, or if you need another swipe of lipstick. No one will be the wiser!

#201. United Raises Credit Card Bonuses To 100,000 Miles—Cardholders Earn More On Flights And Pay Less For Awards

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18 min read (3644 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

United Raises Credit Card Bonuses To 100,000 Miles—Cardholders Earn More On Flights And Pay Less For Awards

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
  • Sources indicate that united and Chase have raised initial bonuses on all four personal credit cards, with offers now reaching 100,000 miles.
  • Sources indicate that I’ve written about United cutting mileage-earning for customers without a card while giving cardholders more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Sources indicate that united and Chase have raised initial bonuses on all four personal credit cards, with offers now reaching 100,000 miles. That’s worth considering because United has made its credit card much harder to skip: eligible primary cardholders earn more miles for flying, then pay fewer miles to book United awards. Even elite status doesn’t eliminate the disadvantage of going without one.

Sources indicate that I’ve written about United cutting mileage-earning for customers without a card while giving cardholders more. If you’re active with the airline and MileagePlus, you need to look at the cost of a card against the miles you’re giving up without it. And with the annual fee cards, you don’t have to put all your spending on one to get the better flight earning and award pricing.

Here’s the current lineup. Each offer has a spending component plus another 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user (an employee card on the business products) within three months of account opening. Card    Initial Bonus    Purchases In First 3 Months    Annual Fee United GatewaySM Card (See rates and fees) 40,000 after $1,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user50,000 total $1,000 $0 UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees) 70,000 after $3,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user80,000 total $3,000 $0 first year, then $150 United QuestSM Card (See rates and fees) 80,000 after $4,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user90,000 total $4,000 $350 United ClubSM Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $695 UnitedSM Business Card (See rates and fees) 90,000 after $5,000 in purchases within 3 months + 10,000 miles for adding an authorized user100,000 total $5,000 $150 There are also elite status incentives: Quest: 500 Premier qualifying points after your first purchase. Business: 2,000 Premier qualifying points after the same $5,000 in purchases within three months that earns the mileage bonus. The extra 10,000 miles for adding a user are awarded once per account, and that user must remain on the account when the bonus is fulfilled. What You’re Giving Up Without A Qualifying Card For United tickets purchased on or after April 2, 2026, here’s what the airline awards for flying. The cardholder column applies to the primary holder of an eligible annual fee card. The United GatewaySM Card requires spending to qualify. MileagePlus Status    Without A Qualifying Card    With A Qualifying Card General member 3 miles per dollar 6 miles per dollar Premier Silver 5 miles per dollar 8 miles per dollar Premier Gold 6 miles per dollar 9 miles per dollar Premier Platinum 7 miles per dollar 10 miles per dollar Premier 1K 9 miles per dollar 12 miles per dollar These rates apply to base airfare and carrier-imposed surcharges and exclude taxes. Basic Economy and other base-option fares have different earning rules. This is mileage earned from flying, separate from whatever the card you use to buy the tickets earns. A general member earns twice as many flight miles with a qualifying card. A 1K doesn’t double their earning, but still picks up three more miles per eligible dollar. Spend $5,000 on eligible fares and that’s 15,000 additional miles at either status level. Then there’s the redemption side. United gives eligible primary cardholders: At least 10% off United and United Express award prices without Premier status. At least 15% off with Premier status. Access to additional Polaris business class Saver award inventory. More seats at the lower price can matter more than the percentage discount. At the minimum discounts, an award with a base price of 100,000 miles becomes 90,000 miles for a cardholder without status, or 85,000 for a cardholder with status. The discounts don’t cover partner-operated flights, Money + Miles bookings, or taxes and fees. You need to book through the primary cardholder’s MileagePlus account. Adding someone as an authorized user doesn’t give their MileagePlus account these benefits. The award pricing benefit can take up to five weeks after card issuance to become available. The No Annual Fee Card Has A $10,000 Spend Requirement To Unlock Benefits United GatewaySM Card‘s offer is 50,000 miles with just $1,000 in purchases and an added authorized user. That’s a record bonus and a low spending requirement. Chase is right to call it the card’s best offer ever. However, Gateway requires $10,000 in purchases in a calendar year to unlock the higher flight earning and cardmember award pricing. Once earned, the award pricing benefit lasts for the rest of that calendar year and the following one. I actually think that UnitedSM Explorer Card (which has a $0 annual fee the first year) and the UnitedSM Business Card are both better options. Which Offer Makes The Most Sense? UnitedSM Explorer Card is the base personal card. You get up to 80,000 miles and the better MileagePlus earning and award prices without a first year annual fee. It also comes with Group 2 boarding, two United Club one-time passes each year, and a free first checked bag for the primary cardholder and one companion on the same reservation. The bag benefit generally requires buying the tickets with the card. Club passes are subject to admission restrictions and capacity. The UnitedSM Business Card is especially attractive if you qualify. It matches the 100,000-mile maximum on the Club cards, adds 2,000 qualifying points, and costs $150 a year. It offers a $125 United travel credit after five United flight purchases of at least $100 each in a calendar year. And you get 5,000 anniversary miles when you also hold a personal Chase United card. United QuestSM Card has strong benefits if you’ll use them. The $350 annual fee buys $200 in United TravelBank cash after opening and at each anniversary, plus a 10,000-mile award flight discount starting at the first anniversary. It also provides 1,000 qualifying points annually starting the calendar year after opening. If the $200 credit replaces airfare you’d otherwise buy, you’re left evaluating $150 of the fee against the remaining benefits and that’s the annual fee of Explorer. The United ClubSM Card is for people who will use the lounges. It has a $695 annual fee and includes United Club membership. #199. Southwest Pilot Calls Out Nationwide Flight Shutdown As A Government Control Plot

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11 min read (2258 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

Southwest Pilot Calls Out Nationwide Flight Shutdown As A Government Control Plot

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pilot, reportedly with Southwest Airlines, says he flew from Cancún to Phoenix without any communications problems.
  • He calls the whole thing “a big farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam.
  • The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pilot, reportedly with Southwest Airlines, says he flew from Cancún to Phoenix without any communications problems. He’s concluded that Friday’s nationwide flight shutdown was a government operation to control people. He calls the whole thing “a massive farce.” He managed to successfully complete his own flight, which was already in the air by the time trouble began, and claims that proves the whole thing was a scam. The video is from @mike4flight, the profile of Mike McHugh. Standing in a parking garage in uniform, he lists the facilities he spoke with and says they all worked fine. Then he offers his theory: So whatever’s going on, I think it’s designed to create fear and disruption and chaos, because that’s how the government gets control of things, controls people. Watch the pilot’s video He never explains how this advances the government’s goal, what additional control it gains, or why it wants that control. Which power are stranded passengers supposed to surrender? The government already decides whether planes can take off. Keeping people at the airport for hours accomplishes what, exactly? And how does costing airlines hundreds of millions of dollars in a day advance its goals? He says “I don’t know what’s going on,” but instead of then keeping quiet he decides to tell the world it’s a government operation. His fight went fine, but that doesn’t mean everything was actually fine. Some communications worked, others didn’t. Radar information could become unreliable even while a pilot could hear a controller. A pilot hears the frequencies he’s assigned at the times he’s using them. That doesn’t say much. The decision to let aircraft already airborne continue while stopping departures isn’t a contradiction. Limiting the number of flights controllers had to work given the conditions they faced made sense. Every landing reduced the workload. Every fresh departure would have added another aircraft needing instructions, separation and handoffs between controllers. Remaining capacity could be reserved for aircraft already flying. Working frequencies and contingency procedures could help bring those flights in without supporting a normal stream of new departures. The FAA’s ground stop rules cover facilities that are only partially unable to provide service. You don’t wait until every radio goes silent before reducing traffic. In fact, depending on when he flew, the ground stop may have helped make his trip uneventful. Fewer planes competing for the remaining capacity would make his experience easier. He may be pointing to the benefit of the restriction as evidence it wasn’t needed in the first place. Friday’s nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and was lifted around 8:15 p.m. It lasted over four hours. By early Saturday morning, there were more than 12,500 cancellations across Friday and Saturday. Looks like some stuck travelers got a concert from the singer of Hoobastank during the national air traffic shut down https://t.co/xWW5yE9JaP — Jennie Taer (@JennieSTaer) November 14, 2026 According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, legacy telecommunications switches and routers became overloaded, producing inconsistent radar information and communications at en route centers and airport approach facilities. He said the newer internet protocol switches hadn’t experienced these problems. The L3Harris-operated FAA telecommunications network carries voice and surveillance information between facilities. Trouble moving that information interrupts a controller’s radio audio and radar display. Apparently the break down came in Cisco 600-series routers manufactured between 2001 and 2006. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin managed to throw Duffy under the bus while trying to defend the administration. Standing beside him at the briefing, Mullin said the apparent problem involved Duffy and the FAA installing patches, equipment and technology that overwhelmed the older system. The new tech was “overwhelming the older system.” Duffy’s defense was that the new equipment hadn’t failed. Watch Markwayne Mullin explain the apparent cause beside Sean Duffy When I reviewed the administration’s modernization plan, I warned that compressing decades of hardware replacements, software integrations and transitions into 36 months brought risks of service disruption. Duffy used the briefing to press Congress for $50 billion. He wants more taxpayer money rather than user fees to prop up an agency that’s failed to modernize with the billions given to it before, without explaining why only money – and not fixing project management, budgeting and leadership at the agency – is all that’s needed. I wouldn’t want this nut case to be the pilot on any flight I happen to be on.

Southwest has way more than their fair share of nut jobs. Case and point.

Airlines pay for FAA “services” by the airport fees and fees (taxes) placed on passenger tickets. General Aviation pays for FAA services with a high “fuel tax”. All of this money goes into the “kitty” for use by the FAA. BUT…Congress (both parties!!) will steal this money for pet projects…kinda like the “bridge to nowhere” in Alaska. The FAA doesn’t/won’t take any advice from the NTSB to fix issues related to aviation safety. The DCA regional jet/Army helicopter crash is a PRIME example of complete incompetence. The NTSB says, “get your communications fixed”, “don’t let helicopters fly in KDCA airspace”. Does the Congress or FAA comply? HELL NO! There are those that proffer “privatizing” the FAA. EVEN WORSE! Canada’s private “FAA” NAV CANADA charges for EVERYTHING. A student wants to shoot “touch & go’s”…there’s a charge to your credit card or FBO. You want to shoot several instrument approaches…same thing. You want to fly cross country…a charge. That’s why Canadian student pilots come to the US for training. While the hourly rate may be higher in USD, it’s offset by not being nickel & dimed to death. If you want to point a finger, point it at both senators and your congressman. THEY are the problem!

Industry observers note that did anyone watch the 1997 movie Conspiracy Theory? Crazy conspiracy theories are nuts, unless they are true. Of course, I think the Southwest Pilot is unlikely in the extreme. However, his theory is more likely than my theory that I am going to win $1 billion in the lottery. Just saying.

More serious comment. Cisco routers from 2001 to 2006. I think that is Window XP level technology. Since then, Microsoft forced me to buy a Windows 7 computer. Then a Windows 10 computer. I am being forces to shop for a Window 11 computer. No wonder the update didn’t work.

Industry observers note that as an IT professional for several decades (financial institutions, oil&gas businesses and supply chain management for the world’s largest food firm), I have never known critical systems to be patched or updated during normal business hours. That just never happens. Don’t know what really happened yesterday nor with the Microsoft outage but the stories that are being told that it was updates gone bad, are lies.

Sources indicate that there is an element of truth. Project 2025 has a section that discusses dismantling the FAA and privatizing the system. And in general, yes, fascist regimes do sow chaos and distrust in existing systems as a form of control over the population.

Back in 1984 Charles Perrow wrote a book called, “Normal Accidents”. His contention is that as systems get more complicated thy are more likely to have points where failures magnify through the tightly coupling of various parts. Eventually these can cascade into a catastrophic collapse of the entire system. These situations may be reduced, and to some extent mitigated with good designs and training, but by the very nature of complexity will still occur in totally unexpected ways. In fact, building in redundancies can sometimes be counter-productive as it makes systems even more complicated and prone to failure.

We may have reached this point in air traffic control, made worse by old equipment and a sluggish bureaucracy that reacts rather than is proactive in avoiding accidents. You don’t need a vast plot (though I admit that I wondered if this was the start of a coup) to have a total system failure. One thing does seem likely, and that is more such events will occur, and without intelligent action they will be more frequent.

#198. Airlines Are Giving Passengers ‘Hoe Bags’—But You May Be Owed More When Your Luggage Goes Missing

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words)
General 🌐 Viewfromthewing

Airlines Are Giving Passengers ‘Hoe Bags’—But You May Be Owed More When Your Luggage Goes Missing

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Viewfromthewing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A Southwest Airlines passenger notes her luggage went missing on a flight to Detroit, and the airline handed her what she calls a “hoe bag”: a plastic bag containing a toothbrush, razor, mouthwash and deodorant.
  • Comedian Delo Brown, who posts as @keepitonthedelo, notes Southwest lost her luggage “last week.” She expected a voucher or some sort of credit.
  • Watch Delo Brown’s Southwest Airlines toiletry kit unboxing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A Southwest Airlines passenger notes her luggage went missing on a flight to Detroit, and the airline handed her what she calls a “hoe bag”: a plastic bag containing a toothbrush, razor, mouthwash and deodorant. “This is a care package for hoes.” Comedian Delo Brown, who posts as @keepitonthedelo, says Southwest lost her luggage “last week.” She expected a voucher or some sort of credit. Instead, she got toiletries to use while they looked for her belongings. “Take this hoe bag and be happy.” Watch Delo Brown’s Southwest Airlines toiletry kit unboxing. Then she starts pulling out the contents. There’s a brush, facial pads and cotton swabs, a toothbrush, a razor, wipes, mouthwash and a tiny deodorant. The razor gets a particularly enthusiastic explanation of what it might be used for. By the end, she’s sold: “This is the best hoe bag I have ever received in my life. This is a caring hoe bag. This is a care package for hoes. I love this. Thank you, Southwest, for my hoe bag.” A “hoe bag” means a bag with the overnight essentials you’d bring when you might wind up spending the night at somebody else’s place. Toothbrush, deodorant, something to clean up with, perhaps fresh underwear. A couple of the better comments: “I used to leave those in the top drawer of nightstand on the other side of my bed.” “Got your hoe bag but still missing a WHOLE BAG.” Other commenters think the plain plastic bag and generic toiletries look more like a hospital admission kit or something handed out in jail. Several compare it to the $148 Skims advent calendar that drew complaints over its inexpensive accessories. These are meant to get you through a night without your checked bag, whether your luggage didn’t arrive or a disrupted trip leaves it somewhere you can’t get to. You’d get the at the baggage service office. And you’ll find them at other airlines, too. In a 2009 comparison of airline overnight kits, Wired actually picked Southwest as best overall. Its kit came in a reusable bag with pockets and a hanging hook, and included Speed Stick, Colgate, Scope, Pert Plus and TRESemmé. That was a much more elaborate kit than the plastic bag in this video. Passengers still need their bags back. Expenses in the meantime may be covered by the credit card they used to purchase the ticket, and airlines have to reimburse reasonable, documented expenses caused by delayed baggage. That can include necessary toiletries and replacement clothing. Hotels can help, too. Ask the front desk before buying a toothbrush, toothpaste, razor, shaving cream or comb. Many have complimentary basics, while deodorant, mouthwash, makeup wipes and other items depend on the property. A hotel’s lobby shop often isn’t the only option. I wrote about “Hyatt Has It” when it debuted in 2013. What I liked was that Hyatt would actually tell guests what was available and invite them to ask. At participating full service hotels, they’d deliver the items, knock and leave the bag on the doorknob. Hyatt still advertises the program, including requests through the World of Hyatt app. Holiday Inn’s “Forget Something?” service can offer complimentary toothbrushes, toothpaste, shaving cream, razors and combs. Of course, some hotels would rather sell you the basics. I covered a stranded Marriott Ambassador member who remarked the Detroit Metro Airport Marriott wanted $12 for deodorant and another $12 for mouthwash. Their shuttle would take him anywhere within a mile, but the drugstore was 1.1 miles away. He moved to a Hyatt Place and got the toiletries for free. The chief financial officer of the world’s largest airline said the carrier is positioning itself to be a “premium” option at the global level.

Speaking at the Skift Aviation Forum in Latest York on Thursday, American CFO Nat Pieper said the airline is investing in and improving its highest leverage points.

“That is an ongoing effort. So many different steps to the travel process. But I think we’ve made good progress. I feel like we’ve got momentum and we’re optimistic about where we’re going,” he remarked.

Customer experience, loyalty, network strength, and premium products will be leading priorities, he added, since they encourage customers to stick with the airline over time.

Pieper also noted the airline is focusing on optimizing operations at LAX.

Industry observers note that “Local yields are better than connecting traffic. If you’re going to win and jump on markets, you’ve got to focus on the local market. That’s what we’re going to do in Los Angeles,” he remarked.

According to recent reports, “It’s going to be a gradual build as we get to the end of ’28, when T4 and T5 will be ready to roll, we’ll have 30 gates there,” he continued. Terminal 4 and 5 are undergoing an extensive $1.6 billion modernization.

When it comes to the financials, Pieper mentioned the best way to maximize cash flow is to invest in the product.

“The ultimate goal for American is generate as much cash flow as we can… You can pay your balance sheet and get it into the shape that you want it, as well as generate enough cash to be able to reinvest in your product and have people continue to want to fly your airline,” he said.

#195. Tech Report: Why Boeing 787 Cockpits Use Electronic Checklists Instead Of Paper

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9 min read (1860 words)

Tech Report: Why Boeing 787 Cockpits Use Electronic Checklists Instead Of Paper

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read | Source: Simpleflying

💡 Key Takeaways
  • An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door.
  • Industry observers note that the Boeing 787 Dreamliner's flight deck is designed around digital information.
  • In a recent development, this is more than a change in presentation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

Industry observers note that the Boeing 787 Dreamliner's flight deck is designed around digital information. Large displays bring together flight data, navigation information, aircraft system indications, and alerts, giving pilots access to information that once appeared across numerous separate instruments and documents. The aircraft’s electronic checklist system follows the same philosophy. Instead of relying solely on printed pages, pilots can access normal and non-normal checklists through the flight deck displays.

In a recent development, this is more than a change in presentation. An electronic checklist can connect checklist procedures with aircraft alerts and, where the system supports it, use aircraft signals to confirm that certain actions have been completed. That can help pilots keep track of a procedure, avoid overlooking steps after an interruption, and manage abnormal situations more systematically. Paper checklists still have an notable role, however. Understanding why Boeing adopted electronic checklists means looking at how they work, what they improve, and where their limitations remain.

Sources indicate that the 787’s electronic checklist system is integrated into the aircraft’s flight deck information environment. It provides access to normal checklists, which cover routine phases of flight, and non-normal checklists, which address situations requiring a specific response. Rather than searching through a paper manual, pilots can select the relevant procedure on a display and work through its instructions in sequence.

Sources indicate that the relationship between the checklist system and the aircraft alerting system is particularly important during non-normal operations. When the aircraft detects a condition that generates an applicable alert, the flight crew can access the associated checklist through the flight deck controls. On the 787, selecting the checklist function can bring up the relevant procedure on a multifunction display. If several alerts have associated checklists, the system can present them for the crew to select. This gives pilots a more direct route from an aircraft indication to the procedure intended to address it.

Industry observers note that electronic checklists can also provide information about whether individual actions have been completed. Some items are designed as closed-loop steps, meaning the system receives a signal from the aircraft that can confirm the required configuration or action. Other items are open-loop steps, which require the pilot to verify completion manually. The distinction matters because an electronic checklist does not automatically know whether every action has been performed simply because a pilot has selected or acknowledged an item.

A closer look at some of the most cutting-edge aircraft in 2026.

Paper checklists are straightforward, familiar, and independent of an aircraft's display systems. They have served flight crews for decades, but they also create practical challenges in a modern cockpit. A pilot must locate the correct page, maintain their place while reading, and ensure that the checklist continues from the correct point after an interruption. During a busy phase of flight, even a small loss of place can require the crew to retrace steps and confirm which actions have already been completed.

In a recent development, an electronic checklist addresses several of these difficulties by keeping the procedure within the flight deck display environment. The crew can access the required checklist without handling a separate document, while the system can provide visual indications of progress. Where aircraft data supports automatic confirmation, the display can also distinguish between an action that has been verified by the system and one that still requires a pilot's confirmation. This reduces some of the administrative work involved in tracking a checklist, although it does not remove the need for careful monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that the move toward electronic checklists also reflects the wider development of flight deck automation. As aircraft systems became more integrated, manufacturers had opportunities to connect operating procedures with alerts and aircraft configuration information. Boeing's work on electronic checklists predates the 787. The manufacturer's development of the technology began decades earlier, with its system evolving through the 1990s and becoming part of the Boeing 777 flight deck. The 787 builds on that broader move toward integrated flight deck information rather than representing the beginning of electronic checklist technology.

One of the most key features of an electronic checklist is the difference between closed-loop and open-loop items. Although both appear within the same procedure, they do not work in the same way. A closed-loop item can receive confirmation from an aircraft system or sensor, while an open-loop item depends on the flight crew to perform and verify the action. Understanding this distinction helps explain why an electronic checklist is more than a digital version of a printed page.

For a closed-loop item, the checklist system can use information from the aircraft to determine whether the required condition has been achieved. For example, if a checklist step requires a particular switch or system configuration, an appropriate aircraft signal may allow the system to recognize that the condition has been met. The checklist indication can then change to show completion. The exact indications and available feedback depend on the aircraft system and the individual checklist item.

Can receive confirmation from aircraft data or a system signal.

Can enhancement when the required condition is detected.

Pilot still monitors the action and system response.

Only works where suitable aircraft feedback is available.

An open-loop item works differently. The system cannot independently confirm that the required action has been carried out, so the pilot must complete the task and verify it. This is crucial for actions that depend on human observation, judgment, or confirmation rather than a signal available to the checklist computer. Electronic presentation does not turn every checklist instruction into an automatically verified action. The crew remains responsible for ensuring that each step has been completed correctly.

The aircraft offers exceptional long-haul capabilities.

Electronic checklists are particularly useful when an aircraft generates a non-normal alert. In these circumstances, pilots may need to identify the condition, locate the applicable procedure, assess the aircraft's status, and carry out a series of actions. The checklist system helps connect the alert with the relevant procedure, reducing the need to search manually through a collection of printed pages while managing other flight deck tasks.

It has been revealed that on the Boeing 787, the electronic checklist system works alongside the aircraft's alerting functions. When an alert has an associated checklist, pilots can use the checklist control to access the procedure on a multifunction display. If more than one alert requires a checklist, the crew can be presented with the available procedures and select the one they need. The system therefore helps organize procedural information, but it does not make operational decisions on behalf of the pilots.

Sources indicate that the display also helps crews monitor progress through a procedure. This is particularly relevant when a checklist is interrupted or when several tasks must be managed at the same time. A clear indication of checklist status can help pilots establish which items have been completed and which remain outstanding. Nevertheless, the crew must continue to monitor the aircraft, communicate effectively, and apply the procedure in the context of the situation. The checklist is a tool for supporting those responsibilities, not a substitute for them.

It has been revealed that electronic checklists offer clear advantages, but they also depend on the availability and correct operation of the aircraft's electronic systems. A display failure, checklist system fault, or loss of relevant system feedback can affect how the crew accesses or completes a procedure. For that reason, paper checklists and approved alternative procedures remain notable parts of the wider operational framework. The presence of an electronic checklist does not mean printed procedures are unnecessary.

The Boeing 787's minimum equipment procedures recognize that the electronic checklist system can be unavailable under specified conditions. If the system is inoperative, the applicable maintenance and operational provisions require it to be deactivated and suitable checklist procedures to be used. There are also provisions for situations in which closed-loop indications are unavailable. In those circumstances, crews may need to use the prescribed line-item override procedures to complete the checklist. These provisions demonstrate that the aircraft has procedures for dealing with checklist system limitations rather than assuming the electronic system will always be available.

Available independently of the checklist display.

Require the crew to locate the relevant procedure.

Can confirm supported aircraft configurations.

Depend on functioning electronic equipment.

Provide an alternative when approved procedures require their use.

Paper procedures also provide another way to access information. They do not rely on the checklist display itself, and they can serve as a practical backup when the approved procedures call for their use. However, paper is not automatically safer or more reliable in every situation. A printed checklist can be misplaced, difficult to manage during a busy phase of flight, or harder to track after an interruption. The key point is that electronic and paper procedures have different strengths, and the aircraft's approved operating documentation determines which method to use in a given circumstance.

Sources indicate that explore the striking Airbus A320 vs. Boeing 737 cockpit differences, from sidesticks to noise, and learn how pilots see these iconic flight decks.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest advantage of an electronic checklist is not simply that it removes paper from the cockpit. Its value comes from how it organizes information and, where the aircraft supports it, connects procedures with aircraft system data. A pilot can access an applicable checklist through the flight deck interface, follow its sequence, and receive confirmation for certain actions. That integration can make checklist management more consistent and help reduce errors associated with losing place or overlooking a step after an interruption.

However, electronic systems introduce their own considerations. Pilots must understand how the checklist interface works, recognize the difference between automatically confirmed and manually verified items, and avoid treating a completed indication as proof that the entire aircraft is in the correct condition. A system can only confirm what its sensors and programmed logic are designed to monitor. It cannot replace the crew's responsibility to assess the aircraft, recognize unexpected conditions and apply sound judgment.

The Boeing 787's electronic checklist system therefore represents an evolution in how flight crews manage procedures, rather than an attempt to remove human involvement. It brings checklists closer to the aircraft information they depend on, provides a structured way to monitor progress and supports access to non-normal procedures when alerts occur. Paper procedures remain part of the operational backup framework, while pilots retain responsibility for every action and verification. The technology has changed how the checklist is presented, but the essential purpose remains the same: ensuring that critical actions are completed, checked, and understood before the flight moves on.

  • The most noticeable difference between premium economy and regular economy class is the amount of personal space available to passengers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, premium economy has become an increasingly popular option for passengers on long-haul flights, offering significantly more comfort than economy class without the considerably higher fares associated with business class. In recent years, the cabin has become an important part of the long-haul products of carriers such as Delta Air Lines, Lufthansa, Emirates, and British Airways. Airlines are also continuing to increase the number of seats on their aircraft, often at the expense of regular economy capacity.

Recent findings suggest that according to Going's 2026 State of Travel report, premium economy was the fastest-growing cabin choice among surveyed travelers, increasing from 16% to 20% in just one year. This growing popularity comes as airlines invest heavily in premium products, while passengers become more willing to pay extra for comfort. However, with premium economy fares generally costing 30% to 100% more than regular economy, what do passengers actually get for the extra money?

The most noticeable difference between premium economy and regular economy class is the amount of personal space available to passengers. On most long-haul aircraft, economy class seats have a pitch of approximately 30 to 32 inches (76 to 81 cm), compared to around 38 to 40 inches (97 to 102 cm) in premium economy. Seat pitch is the distance between the same point on two consecutive rows of seats, meaning passengers generally get around seven to nine additional inches of space between seats.

Premium economy seats are also considerably wider than those found in economy class. While regular economy seats typically measure between 17 and 18 inches (43 to 46 cm), premium economy seats are often between 18.5 and 19.5 inches (47 to 50 cm) wide. Most airlines also provide additional recline, generally between six and eight inches (15 to 20 cm), and many seats feature adjustable headrests, calf rests, and footrests. These differences become particularly noticeable on overnight flights, where passengers may spend eight to 12 hours in the same seat.

However, the actual differences depend on the airline and aircraft type. Lufthansa's new Allegris premium economy product, for example, offers 39 inches (99 cm) of seat pitch and features a fixed-shell design that lets passengers recline without disturbing the person behind them. Other carriers, including Emirates and Cathay Pacific, offer premium economy seats with up to 40 inches of pitch, while certain airlines provide even more space.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Besides the extra space, most airlines include other benefits for passengers traveling in premium economy. On long-haul flights, this often includes upgraded meal services, a wider selection of drinks, and better-quality amenities than those provided in regular economy. Depending on the airline, passengers may receive a welcome drink before departure, meals served on proper tableware, noise-canceling headphones, and an amenity kit. Many airlines have also installed larger inflight entertainment screens and additional power outlets in their premium economy seats.

Emirates, for example, provides its premium economy passengers with upgraded dining, including meals served on proper tableware, along with larger entertainment screens and more personal space. Lufthansa has also improved its premium economy offering through its Allegris product, introducing wireless charging, additional storage compartments, and privacy features. These investments are part of a broader effort to differentiate premium economy from regular economy rather than simply selling passengers a seat with additional legroom.

The differences also extend to the airport experience, as many airlines provide priority check-in and boarding. Moreover, premium economy fares often include a larger checked baggage allowance than economy tickets. However, these benefits can vary considerably depending on the airline and fare type, and lounge access is generally not included. For example, some airlines offer lower-priced premium economy fares with reduced baggage allowances, so passengers should not assume every premium economy ticket includes the same benefits.

Sources indicate that it is also crucial to distinguish premium economy from extra-legroom economy products, such as United Airlines' Economy Plus. While these seats generally provide more legroom, passengers still receive the same basic seat and onboard service as regular economy travelers. Dedicated premium economy cabins, such as United Premium Plus or Delta Premium Select, offer wider seats and a different onboard product. However, unlike modern business class suites, these seats do not convert into fully flat beds.

It seems to be one of the use of space aboard aircraft for maximizing revenue.

Premium economy is generally considerably more expensive than a regular economy class ticket, with passengers often paying between 30% and 100% more for the additional comfort and services. However, the actual difference depends heavily on the airline, route, and time of booking. While the upgrade can sometimes be relatively affordable, particularly on longer flights, premium economy fares can also approach those of discounted business class tickets.

In a recent development, to put these differences into perspective, Simple Flying previously compared British Airways' premium economy and business class fares on three of the airline's busiest transatlantic routes from London Heathrow Airport (LHR). The analysis, conducted on May 25, 2026, examined one-way fares to New York, Boston, and Los Angeles for travel during July 2026 and February 2027.
