#157. Tech Report: When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

📅 23 Dec 2024 • ⏱️ 10 min read (2064 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

Tech Report: When to Visit Machu Picchu for Clear Views and Fewer Crowds

📅 23 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind.
  • It has been revealed that the drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours.
  • Sources indicate that for a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You may already have a clear picture of a trip to Machu Picchu long before you have a date to go in mind. On a first visit, you want time to take in the massive scale of the Inca city on its forested ridge above the Urubamba River, and then to walk among its stone walls. That picture, of course, depends on the weather. Here, where the Andes fall away toward the Amazon basin, a single bank of cloud can hide Waynapicchu, the peak behind the ruins, and with it the panorama you came to see.

It has been revealed that the drier months improve the odds of a clear view, but draw more visitors with similar dreams to the same routes and entry hours. The weeks just after the rains offer greener slopes—and often thinner crowds—to anyone prepared to pack for showers. The best time to visit Machu Picchu comes down to matching the conditions to the type of visit you want, as well as confirming that your route is available before you commit to booking trains and rooms. Below are the questions that first-time visitors ask most, with advice from travel advisors and experts.

Sources indicate that for a first visit, May and September—before and after the June-to-August rush, respectively—will have generally favorable walking weather, before the rains creep back in October. The two months aren’t interchangeable, especially if you hope to walk to the Sun Gate or the Inca Bridge. The 2026 route calendar opened those seasonal paths in September but not in May, so check the 2027 dates as soon as they’re published.

April brings greener slopes to anyone who can live with a little more water. “It’s also shoulder season so there aren’t many tourists yet,” says Alice Farkas, who leads marketing and communications at Aracari, a company based in Lima that aims private trips across South America. Kiernan Cochran, product manager at Andean, which plans trips throughout Peru, also favors April into early May. Even so, Cochran’s team books those weeks for travelers with much the same lead time as high season, since popular routes fill early.

When it comes to visiting Machu Picchu, daily timing might matter even more than which time of year you visit.

November through March offers significant savings on airfare and accommodations, though strategic planning remains essential. Permits for popular routes like Huayna Picchu still require three-month advance booking during these months (compared to six months of required lead time during peak season).

Mosquera makes a case for embracing the rainy season: "It's actually my favorite time. The site becomes magical with fewer crowds given that overtourism is one of Machu Picchu's greatest threats. The rain isn't nearly as disruptive as people imagine, as it mainly falls in the evenings, not all day. February is particularly special because the Inca Trail closes for maintenance, making the site even quieter." (Note: If you blueprint to arrive by trek, options will be more limited during these moments.).

According to recent reports, the wet season transforms the landscape dramatically. Stone terraces flush vibrant green, hidden waterfalls emerge, and morning mist creates atmospheric reveals of the citadel. The timing also aligns perfectly with Peru's coastal summer. "More travelers are discovering this split-season strategy," states Mosquera. "You can explore misty ruins early in the trip, then travel down to Lima's world-class restaurants or Máncora's beaches where summer's in full swing." Temperatures at Machu Picchu remain moderate year-round, with rain typically following predictable afternoon patterns rather than all-day downpours.

In a recent development, the dry months from June through August draw the main crush of tourists, when the most desirable entry hours can sell out along with hotels and trains. Inti Raymi, the Inca Festival of the Sun, culminates in Cusco on June 24, and Peru’s Independence Day on July 28 brings another surge. In 2026, the daily cap was 4,500 visitors on ordinary dates and 5,600 on specified days, including June 19 through November 2, though that calendar doesn’t automatically carry over to 2027. Those places are also divided by route and hour, so your preferred route and entry time may be full even when the site has space overall.

Once each year’s tickets are released, Andean suggests booking sought-after routes about six months ahead in high season and at least three months ahead in low season.

Allow four or five nights in the region, as Cochran recommends, and begin in the Sacred Valley if your itinerary allows. Its Inca towns and terraces also mean the citadel isn’t your first encounter with the culture that built it. Cusco, where flights land for now, sits at roughly 11,150 feet. Heading straight down to the valley gives you a gentler start, and you can return to explore the city afterward. Cusco’s long-delayed replacement airport, Chinchero International, is under construction on the plateau above the Sacred Valley at about 12,340 feet, higher than the city itself. Its opening is targeted for late 2027, so most 2027 trips will still begin at the old one.

Ollantaytambo, at about 9,160 feet, is halfway between Cusco and Machu Picchu, and where travelers board the train to the latter. The town of ‘Ollanta’ has Inca-era streets and archaeological sites to explore, and is well worth a stop either going to or coming from Machu Picchu (the lovely El Albergue hotel sits just beside the train station).

From there, travelers catch the train to Aguas Calientes, also known as Machu Picchu Pueblo, which is the small town at the base of the ancient citadel. Spend the night prior to your Machu Picchu visit in Aguas Calientes for an early start up the mountain. Some allow just one day at Machu Picchu; others who want to appreciate the landmark from a few perspectives should budget two. You may, for instance, want to experience an upper terrace or a mountain climb alongside Classic Circuit 2, which is the standard walk through the Inca city (more on these routes below). If so, book that second route for another day. Either way, you can usually spend a full day at Machu Picchu and still catch a late afternoon/early evening train out, or bed down for another night in Aguas Calientes and depart the next morning.

Industry observers note that before buying anything sold simply as “Machu Picchu admission,” take a look at the official route maps, since the three circuits divide the site by elevation and access. For a single visit, Andean favors Classic Circuit 2. Its routes 2-A and 2-B each pair a viewpoint with a walk among the Inca buildings of the urban sector. Route 2-B takes its view from the lower terrace, a distinction worth knowing if you have a particular camera angle in mind.

For the upper-terrace panorama, choose Circuit 1’s route 1-B, which keeps you above the main streets, while route 1-A adds the climb up Machu Picchu Mountain which offers the classic view down onto the site. The Sun Gate and Inca Bridge carry seasonal tickets of their own. Circuit 3 covers the lower royal sector, including the Temple of the Sun. Its route 3-A adds the steep ascent of Waynapicchu (often spelled Huayna Picchu), which is the distinctive peak in the background of most Machu Picchu photos, and 3-B stays below. If Circuit 2 sells out, Andean suggests booking Circuits 1 and 3 separately to combine the panorama with a closer look at the ruins. Choose wisely before you arrive, since a ticket cannot be switched to another route at the gate.

Hikers face their own paperwork. Permits for the classic Inca Trail are limited and booked through authorized operators, and the shorter one-day trail from kilometer 104 of the rail line needs a permit and an operator, too. That day hike is Cochran’s own favorite—the final leg of the historic Inca route to the Sun Gate, without the multiday inn-to-inn or camping journey required. Ask what your hike covers before buying a separate admission.

Under the September 2026 rules, trail arrivals enter on a designated Circuit 3-B ticket, which matters if you also want Circuit 2 or the upper panorama. Heavy rain can also shut the kilometer 104 path outside the usual February maintenance period, which is something to keep in mind for any rainy season travel.

In a recent development, your train booking does not include admission (treks are on a case-by-case basis; ask!), so buy entry through the Ministry of Culture’s Tu Boleto portal, where you choose your route first and your entry hour second. Enter each visitor’s details carefully, matching names and information to the same identification document they’ll present at the gate. The ticket fixes the holder’s name, date, time, and route; current rules allow no changes to the name or date after purchase.

Industry observers note that the purchase process changed in September 2026, when the ministry began a 30-day trial of direct paid checkout in place of the earlier unpaid hold. Under the portal’s current purchase manual, you have 15 minutes from the start of an order to enter everyone’s details and pay. Have documents and payment ready, and follow the instructions on screen. Rail and admission are also released on separate timelines. PeruRail opened 2027 train sales on September 22, but Yuriko Aquino of PROMPERÚ, Peru’s tourism promotion agency, states the Ministry of Culture has yet to announce when 2027 admission will go on sale or what the daily visitor cap will be. If you buy rail first, read the fare’s change terms before you pay.

Recent findings suggest that within the overall cap, up to 1,000 tickets a day are held for in-person sale in Machu Picchu Pueblo, valid for entry the following day. If you’re counting on that uncertain fallback, budget a night in town. Whichever way you buy, a guide is recommended for a standard citadel visit, while Inca Trail hikers follow their operator’s separate requirements. Guides can be booked through your hotel or at the entrance to the site.

It has been revealed that from Cusco, most travelers cross the Sacred Valley by road to Ollantaytambo and board the train there for the ride along the Urubamba to Machu Picchu Pueblo. From town, a separate shuttle bus climbs to the entrance in roughly half an hour. Check boarding points and total travel time before choosing a fare, since PeruRail’s January-to-April departures from Cusco involve a bus-and-train transfer.

For a first visit, Cochran favors a morning train from the Sacred Valley and an afternoon Circuit 2 entry, when her team generally finds the site less crowded; three or four hours is usually enough to take it in. Among the premium trains, she points to Belmond’s Hiram Bingham, PeruRail’s Vistadome Observatory, and IncaRail’s First Class.

Whichever train you choose, leave a cushion between arrival and admission. Peru’s tourism authority advises reaching the shuttle station about an hour before your gate slot, or setting out about two hours ahead if you plan to walk uphill. A train that pulls in just before your entry time leaves little margin for the bus queue and the gate check.

Recent findings suggest that down in Machu Picchu Pueblo are two fantastic Peruvian-owned options—Inkaterra Machu Picchu Pueblo Hotel, with scattered adobe casitas among orchids, and Sumaq Machu Picchu Hotel, which faces the Urubamba River. Both are close to the shuttle stop. Sanctuary Lodge, a Belmond Hotel, is the only property up on the mountain at the gates of Machu Picchu, which spares you the morning shuttle ascent, though hotel guests still enter on the same timed admission as everyone else.

These Music City Airbnbs Exude All of Nashville’s Southern Charm

📅 14 Jun 2019 | ⏱️ 12 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the two decades I’ve lived in Nashville, I’ve seen a lot of changes. When I first moved, my friends and family would ask why I lived here; now, they’re asking when they can come visit. And as the Music City grows, so does the number of gorgeous places to stay. Travelers can choose from vacation rentals in any neighborhood for any group size, whether that be large bachelorette parties looking to hang out near the honky-tonks, or solo music lovers who want to catch a show at the Grand Ole Opry. Houses with vast yards are good options for folks with kids, dogs, and songwriter friends who want to pull out the guitar, and some even boast private pools that let you keep the summer heat at bay. Nashville, of course, is known for its street of honky-tonks, and securing a modern condo downtown with a bird’s-eye view of all the action offers a one-of-a-kind experience that you won’t soon forget. No matter what type of stay you’re after, there’s an excellent Nashville vacation rental worth holing up in. Read on for some of my favorite vacation rentals in the city I call home.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, editor stays, ratings, amenities, location, decor, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Cozy fireplace, roomy layout, spacious yard, large dining table.

Comfortable and quiet, this family-ready home in South Nashville will make you feel like a true local. With four bedrooms—three kings and a room with bunk beds for kids—all dressed in modern, neutral tones; two baths; and a dog-friendly policy, the whole family will enjoy a stay here. There’s even a dedicated workspace if you have to check in with the office while on the road. It’s an oasis slightly away from all the noise and activity that downtown brings, but just a short drive from any late-night action you desire.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds; Adventure Science Center; Zanies’ comedy club; bars, restaurants, and shopping in Wedgewood-Houston.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Shou Sugi Ban traditional Japanese design, peaceful location, firepit.

According to recent reports, just 16 miles away from downtown Nashville, this bed-and-breakfast tree house on 22 wooded acres can feel worlds away from Lower Broadway and the neon honky-tonk nightlife. But in half an hour, you could be back in the center of the action, should you want to be. It’s the perfect spot for those who like to balance their major-city trips with a bit of solitude and relaxation after a long day. At home, expect great views, a delicious breakfast, and the chance to truly disconnect—there’s no Wi-Fi or TV.

Location: Ashland CityThings to do nearby: Hiking trails on property, Beaman Park, Cumberland River kayaking.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Photogenic pink backdrop, free parking, wood-fired pizza oven, outdoor projector, guitar, local landlords.

East Nashville’s self-named “Nashville Pinky” is bedecked in a paler pink than some other properties in the city, but it doesn’t scale back when it comes to making Music City fun. Spend the day at home watching movies on the outdoor projector and eating pizza from the wood-fired oven. There’s also a guitar if you want to pick your way through some songs, and vinyl records from the nearby record shop, The Groove. When you’re ready to head out, the neighborhood is full of bars, boutiques, and restaurants, and you’re a quick bus ride, bike ride, or Uber from Lower Broadway.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Five Points bars and restaurants, Shoppes on Fatherland, the Basement East music venue, Shelby Park.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private parking, stock tank tub, electric fireplace, cozy loft space.

In a recent development, finding a pet-friendly Airbnb isn't as easy as it seems, as many homes come with extensive rules regarding what Fido can and can't do, and high nightly fees in addition to the booking price. This two-bedroom guesthouse sits in a middle ground: There's a $75 fee per small or medium dog, who will have to hang out in a crate if you leave them home alone. There's a small backyard for your pup to explore (with a firepit for humans), and the neighborhood has wide sidewalks for safe, on-leash adventures. The tchotchke-filled home itself is best for families, since the primary bedroom lacks a true door, and the secondary bedroom has twin beds. Inside, there's also a kitchenette with an oven, mini-fridge, and coffee maker, and an indoor fireplace to curl up in front of.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Salt Ranch pool club, Cleveland Park shopping, bars and restaurants, Drkmttr music venue.

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Relaxing atmosphere, private connected apartment for more space, substantial deck, private parking.

According to recent reports, the unofficial bachelorette capital of the world, Nashville is a hot spot for group trips—especially for women. And while the rowdier set may be found on Broadway driving past the honky-tonks in “party barges,” there's a more, well, sophisticated way to celebrate upcoming nuptials. To start, book this 1930s East Nashville cottage that's away from the crowds and has an explicit “no parties” rule. With two bedrooms in the main house plus a third in the connected apartment, and two queen-size sofa beds, there's plenty of room to spread out. Outside, the home has a backyard, two-level deck, grill, and firepit. Plus, you're only 10 minutes from downtown if you want to get in on the honky-tonk action.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Cumberland River kayaking; Shelby Park; Five Points restaurants, bars, and shopping; The Basement East music venue.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Chocolate-themed decor, location in a multi-use complex with a coffee shop and a chocolatier, blackout shades.

Sources indicate that you’ll definitely have sweet dreams when you stay in this chocolatier-owned apartment next door to her high-end chocolate shop. The rooms at Cocoa Casa are bright, colorful, and decorated with chocolate-themed decor, without being over-the-top or hokey. You can head next door to sample the goods from Poppy and Peep Chocolate (or take them home as souvenirs). The South Nashville location is within walking distance of coffee shops and more, but offers a little less hustle-and-bustle than the downtown scene.

Location: South NashvilleThings to do nearby: International food along Nolensville Pike; Wedgewood-Houston’s restaurants, bars, and luxury shops; Geodis Park (the MLS stadium); the Nashville Fairgrounds.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound porch, seasonal in-ground pool, piano, view of Shelby Park, bunk beds.

This beautifully designed East Nashville farmhouse may come with a large price tag for a two-bedroom, two-bath home, but its location and heated pool (open April to October) are well worth it. Facing Shelby Park—and close to the greenway, which is packed with walking and jogging trails—the home is just 10 minutes from downtown Nashville. There's a wraparound porch to enjoy your morning coffee, plus hammocks and bikes to take in the fresh air. Inside, the bright white design gives the home a fresh, clean look. (If you have a massive group, there are a few air mattresses available, and the hosts allow up to eight guests.).

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: Kayaking; golfing; Shelby Park; Shelby Bottoms Nature Center; Five Points bars, restaurants, and shopping.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Location on a working organic farm, views of Tennessee hills, gourmet kitchen, farm animals.

Recent findings suggest that if you're a Nashville regular, it may be time to look outside of the city for your next vacation. About 30 minutes south of Nashville International Airport, this rental on Bloomsbury Farm is just far enough away to feel like a retreat, but not too far that you can't head into the city every day. It's also perfectly located for a visit to Franklin (a 20-minute drive), one of my favorite day trips from the city, and Arrington Vineyards for wine tasting. Set on over 400 acres of working farmland, the loft is kitted out with a full kitchen, living area, bathroom with a walk-in shower, and king-size bedroom, all overlooking the Tennessee hills. Bonus: The farm has turkeys, horses, and chickens—so if you're lucky, your host will pass on a few fresh eggs for your morning breakfast.

Location: SmyrnaThings to do nearby: Bloomsbury Farm tour, wooded paths, Smyrna Depot District, boat rentals at Fate Sanders Marina.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows; private balcony; access to laundry, pool, and gym in building; central location.

In a recent development, A sleek, modern pied-à-terre, this apartment offers floor-to-ceiling windows with city views, complemented by leather and metal furnishings and a few scene-stealing art pieces, like the LED angel wings. It all adds up to a great photo op for the whole crew on a memorable Nashville vacation. Make use of the year-round heated pool and fitness center, and then walk a few blocks to Lower Broadway for the honky-tonk action. The home can sleep up to six across a king bedroom, queen bedroom, and pull-out sofa bed in the living room.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum, Lower Broadway honky-tonks, Bridgestone Arena, Nashville Symphony Schermerhorn Symphony Center.

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, laundry room, welcoming decor, large backyard, budget-friendly prices.

In a recent development, the real perks of this serene East Nashville cottage are outside: The backyard offers space for kids to wear themselves out running around while you sit on the back patio, taking a breather. Inside, the two-bedroom home has a washer/dryer, room-darkening shades, and a bathtub. It's only about a 10-minute drive to downtown Nashville and 15 minutes from the Grand Ole Opry. And best of all, you can score it for under $200 a night.

Location: East NashvilleThings to do nearby: TopGolf; Salt Ranch pool club; Cleveland Park shopping, bars, and restaurants; Drkmttr music venue; Nissan Stadium.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Access to laundry, early luggage drop-off, elevator access, high ceilings.

This industrial loft is among a variety of rentals in one of downtown Nashville's century-old buildings—and is run by local firm Anchor Rentals, which also manages The Russell, a boutique hotel in a renovated East Nashville church. What that means for business travelers headed here is that they won't have to worry about the hosts canceling or not being in the area. This particular apartment, with its high ceilings, multiple workspaces, and well-equipped kitchen (which includes a microwave, coffee machine, and toaster oven for quick breakfasts), is a great spot for weekday visitors.

Location: Downtown NashvilleThings to do nearby: Ryman Auditorium, Lower Broadway, Frist Art Museum, Dolly Museum Nashville.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pack-and-play, toys for kids, minimalist design, groovy bar cart, French press coffee.

Recent findings suggest that perfectly located 15 minutes away from both Vanderbilt and Belmont University on foot, this apartment in Music Row is an easy home base for parents visiting collegians or touring with high schoolers. With two bedrooms and one bathroom, it has enough space to comfortably fit four people. (If you're traveling with toddlers or infants, the home also offers a pack-and-play and children's books and toys.) There's also a full kitchen complete with a gorgeous Smeg fridge.

Location: Music RowThings to do nearby: Studio B; Vanderbilt University; Belmont University; restaurants, bars and shops in Hillsboro Village and Edgehill Village; Belcourt Theatre.

What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Nashville?

East Nashville and Wedgewood-Houston are two busy and buzzy neighborhoods with great dining scenes, music venues, and fun shopping. They’re also a quick Uber or bike ride to downtown, making it easy to experience it all. If you’re looking for something a bit quieter, check out the leafy Sylvan Park neighborhood. For something fit for families, head to Donelson, with easy access to parks and the Opryland attractions.

When is the best season to visit Nashville?

Industry observers note that there’s no bad time to visit Nashville, but spring and fall offer more temperate weather, when it is easier to hike, bike, and paddle, or just stroll down Broadway without the steaminess of a southern summer collecting under your hat. Most people want to be in Music City during the warmer months to take advantage of outdoor concerts and street festivals, but if you come in winter, you’ll get to cheer on the NHL’s Nashville Predators and see the holiday magic of the five million lights at Gaylord Opryland.

In a recent development, in my opinion, a trip to Nashville should be about five days long, which offers you enough time to expand your vacation beyond Broadway and the honky-tonks. You’ll have enough time for a day or two in town—you can boot-scoot under the neon lights of Lower Broadway—and still have a few days for exploring the surrounding parks, greenways, museums, shops, and music venues away from the crowds.

Singapore Airlines Unveils the ‘Largest Double Bed in the Sky’ As Part of a $1.6 Billion Redesign

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class.
  • The airline confirmed the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.
  • Singapore Airlines's newly introduced first class cabin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting a good night's sleep on a long-haul flight isn't easy, even when you're lucky enough to be flying first class. But Singapore Airlines—consistently voted as one of the best airlines in the world by CNT readers—is taking things to a whole upcoming level, unveiling what it claims will be “the largest double bed in commercial aviation” as part of a major revamp of its long-haul cabins.

The airline confirmed the $1.6 billion redesign on Friday, November 6, with the first aircraft expected to enter service in the second half of 2027.

Singapore Airlines's newly introduced first class cabin.

In a recent development, the biggest change is coming to first class, where passengers traveling together will be able to transform two adjoining seats into a double bed measuring 80 inches long and 60 inches wide—the same size as a standard queen bed in the US. The seats can also be converted into a two-person sofa, while curved sliding doors and retractable dividers will offer additional privacy.

And the luxury doesn't stop there. The upcoming suites will feature Italian Poltrona Frau leather upholstery, personal wardrobes, dedicated dining spaces, and 32-inch 4K entertainment screens. Passengers can also expect proper bedding, including cotton sheets, duvets, a choice of pillows, and mattress toppers from German bedding specialist Paradies.

The latest business class seats also come with adjoining seats, offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion.

It has been revealed that business class passengers won't be left out either. Redesigned seats will come with sliding privacy doors, improved lumbar support and fully flat beds, with selected adjoining seats offering the option to sleep alongside a traveling companion. Smart controls in both premium cabins will even remember passengers' preferred seating positions for future flights.

Recent findings suggest that but what about those of us traveling farther back? Premium economy will benefit from additional personal space, adjustable leg rests, dedicated storage, and larger entertainment screens. Meanwhile, economy passengers can look forward to redesigned seats with more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The fresh economy class will feature more leg space, adjustable headrests, and new storage compartments.

The upgrades will be introduced gradually across Singapore Airlines's new Boeing 777-9 aircraft and 41 retrofitted Airbus A350-900 aircraft, including its ultra-long-range fleet. The latter will also receive first class cabins for the first time.

There's no confirmed date yet for when passengers will be able to try the fresh double beds, but one thing is certain: cuddling up at 35,000 feet has just become a little more appealing.

JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown.

The boutique air carrier intends to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts.

According to recent reports, the Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response.

It has been revealed that JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Notably, JSX did not specify which Upcoming York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies.

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program.

“Greater Boston represents an exciting upcoming chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an crucial milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox noted in a statement.

“As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added.

Sources indicate that JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

According to recent reports, the public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns.

Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight.

JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February.

With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York.

Giosue Vezzuto Appointed CEO of RINA Services

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Cruiseindustrynews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Giosue Vezzuto has been appointed chief executive officer of RINA Services, the RINA Group company active in marine and certification services.
  • RINA remarked that Vezzuto has led the manufacturer since August, succeeding Paolo Moretti, who today serves as chief executive officer and general manager of RINA S.p.A..
  • Vezzuto said: “I take on this role with pride and determination, and I am grateful for the trust placed in me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giosue Vezzuto has been appointed chief executive officer of RINA Services, the RINA Group company active in marine and certification services.

RINA remarked that Vezzuto has led the manufacturer since August, succeeding Paolo Moretti, who today serves as chief executive officer and general manager of RINA S.p.A..

Vezzuto said: “I take on this role with pride and determination, and I am grateful for the trust placed in me. Over the past five years, we have achieved average annual growth of 15 percent in Marine and 10 percent in Certification.”.

In a recent development, “These results reflect the dedication of our people and the trust our clients continue to place in RINA. I am committed to building on this progress with ambition, focusing on the quality of our results and services and fostering innovation that creates tangible value for our clients and our people,” added Vezzuto.

“Throughout, we will remain firmly anchored in the values that define us: competence, independence and reliability.”.

Moretti added: “Over the years, I have had the opportunity to appreciate Vezzuto’s vision and capabilities across the various roles he has held in Italy and internationally, and I am confident that his experience will bring further value to the markets in which RINA Services operates.”.

“With his leadership, the expertise of our people and the strong foundations built over the years, RINA Services is well positioned to continue its growth and make an even stronger contribution to the group’s development.”.

According to recent reports, RINA noted RINA Services generated revenues of over €384 million in 2025, representing around 37 percent of the Group’s total revenues and a 13 percent year-on-year increase. The firm expects revenues to exceed €400 million in 2026.

A naval engineer by training, Vezzuto joined RINA in 1997 and has built his career within the group, holding a range of managerial, commercial and operational roles of increasing responsibility.

He started in classification and engineering before moving to the Marine business unit.

He has served as deputy manager of the Naples office, head of the Singapore office, country manager for Southeast Asia, regional manager for Northern Europe and regional manager for Asia.

Since 2019, he has served as executive vice president, Marine, at RINA Services.

#149. 14 Best Steakhouses in Upcoming York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

📅 14 Dec 2024 • ⏱️ 13 min read (2615 words)
General 🌐 Cntraveler

14 Best Steakhouses in Upcoming York City for Old-School Chops, Wagyu, and the Perfect Martini

📅 14 Dec 2024 | ⏱️ 13 min read | Source: Cntraveler

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that no single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC.
  • Read our complete Upcoming York City guide here, which includes:.
  • It has been revealed that I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel vital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that no single steakhouse can beat out all the others in NYC. Each has its strengths, and some are certainly better than others. There are the classics—Keens and Gallaghers in Midtown, Delmonico's in the Financial District, Peter Luger over in Williamsburg—that have been here for a hundred years or more, and for good reason. They are dimly-lit, tavern-like, with walls clad in wood. The menus do not change. The new and newish guard variously emulate and do their own thing. Increasingly, we are seeing steakhouses taking the basic assignment—red meat and sides in a formal dining room—and running with it in various cultural directions. Below, we've rounded up our favorites across this board. What's most important is their shared ability to make its diner feel important, a feat that goes beyond (but does require) the ability to gorge on good steak.

Read our complete Upcoming York City guide here, which includes:.

Seagram Building, 99 E 52nd St, Midtown Manhattan.

It has been revealed that I am forming the opinion that a steakhouse's cardinal function is to make its diners feel vital. No place has succeeded so impeccably in this mission as The Grill, where I was whisked from a downstairs lobby into the glamorous dining room as though a visiting board member come to town to be courted and impressed. I went for lunch, so the metal chain curtains that undulate (yes, they are ever-moving) over the massive windows shimmered in the daylight. Everyone except for me, it seemed, as there on very important business. I was the only male diner that I could see not in a jacket. The menu is very spendy (you cannot get a cocktail for less than $26) and therefore especially reserved for special occasions. Peppered filet mignon and martini, I'd say, are the way to go, but if it's lunch and the prime rib roast beef sandwich is being served, it's a worthy detour. —C.H.

The best thing that happened to me at 4 Charles Prime Rib was that I made a fresh friend. Steak and martinis and burgers, they're all fabulous—make no mistake. But sometimes it’s the life that comes at you in pursuit of those delicious menu items that leaves you feeling the most full. Too corny? Allow me to elaborate.

According to recent reports, 4 Charles is one of the toughest tables in town. Like Torrisi, it’s practically a private members' club where the only people who can land a reservation are those who’ve eaten there before. Hopeful walk-ins start lining up over an hour before opening at 4 p.m., and I got there at 2:45 p.m. to find myself second in line. I sat on the West Village townhouse stoop and enjoyed the day, enjoyed the sight of the staff puttering around setting up, glared at the people with reservations who we in line agreed were “line cutters.” When the host began seating people around 3:45 p.m., she told me that I was the first single walk-in and would therefore enjoy the one table by the door that they reserve for such parties. The man behind me, who arrived nary five minutes after I did, was told he would therefore have to wait until I was done. “Can’t I just sit with him?” he asked in earnest bewilderment. “Sure!” I responded.

It has been revealed that and so together we unhinged our jaws and ate the 10-ounce double wagyu smash burger with thick slabs of bacon, his with an egg, and together we poured the beef jus over the pink center of the titular 4 Charles Cut and expressed our unexpected delight with the horseradish cream accoutrement. Together we drank martinis—I, a perfect vesper; he, an espresso; and then a chocolate each. If you’re going to try to go, I recommend you do so in this way. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor.

Peter Luger isn't just the Brooklyn steakhouse. It just might be the Latest York City steakhouse, especially if history carries any weight with you, dear reader. This fine establishment has sat at the same address in the Williamsburg Bridge's shadow since 1887, and the interiors carry about as many frills as your average public house—dark wood, plaster walls, and so on. The menu is just as unadorned, with the most popular menu items being the dry-aged steak for two, steak for three, or steak for four. You can also, rest assured, get a single steak, lamb chops, salmon, or filet of sole. The Luger's sizzling bacon is not to be missed, nor are the sliced tomatoes and onions with Luger's Own sauce (pro tip: they go quite well together.) If you're there before 3:45 p.m., you'd also be wise to order the over-½-lb Luger burger, which is so simple and bloody with optional American cheese that your eyes will roll back in your head. —C.H.

Industry observers note that this summer, the Montecito and Malibu staple Lucky's Steakhouse came to roost on a bustling street in New York’s Soho—and has been a fun addition to the city’s oft-stodgy steakhouse landscape ever since. Importantly, it’s a cool counterpoint—with its intimate size, Jazz Age-y murals, sexy date-night vibe, and a menu that accommodates non-steak eaters (i.e. me, a pescatarian). I know what you’re thinking: Why is a non-meat eater reviewing Lucky’s? Well, precisely for the fact that steakhouses can be wincingly non-inclusive, despite often being the restaurant of choice on special occasions. And Lucky’s feels different, not least because of its ambience. On a recent night, we started with the oysters, the peaky-toe crab cocktail, house chips, and Jimmy’s Greek salad (named after a family member of the owner). I then got the salmon, initially a perverse choice—because it usually plays poor country cousin at most steakhouses—but it was excellent. And we really dug into the sides—onion rings, market vegetables, and creamed corn. Both times I ate there, my companions ordered the 10-oz Gene’s Filet and I heard murmurs of firm approval. Whatever your dietary preference, don’t miss Lucky’s martini service, for which multiple servers will shake (or stir) your drinks table-side and in unison—because a little theatre hurts no one.

In a recent development, head 10 blocks south of Newly introduced York’s Koreatown (see an itinerary of the neighborhood here), and you'll find Cote, a Korean steakhouse and one of the city’s best and buzziest restaurants. There’s no shortage of a la carte options, but the prix-fixe Butcher’s Feast is where diners should start. For $74 a person, you're treated to seasonal ban-chan, savory egg soufflé, two stews (including spicy kimchi stew), and the house selection of beef, including USDA Prime and Wagyu, cooked on the table with smokeless grills. The restaurant’s award-winning wine list features an impressive Champagne selection, and all by-the-glass pours come from Magnums, the large-format bottles that sommeliers say keeps wines younger and fresher. There's also a second location at 550 Madison that's a bit grander, should that suit you. —D.F.

Industry observers note that gallaghers is the best steakhouse to eat at before a Broadway show. Wood paneled walls covered in framed old photographs (one of singer Perry Comon had to be labeled “this is not Jeffrey Epstein” due to those two men’s shared resemblance) offset the inhumane Midtown environment just beyond the front door. This is a place that’s as good for steak (and it really is good for steak) as it is for all of the accoutrements one expects of a good steakhouse—beyond the bovine, highlights include the old fashioned, the creamed spinach, the house-smoked bacon, and the beautifully browned veal chop parmigiana. Putting it all over the edge is the people watching—real live businesspeople drowning their sorrows at the bar alongside the theatergoers, and haughty waiters doing buttoned-up to the max. —C.H.

The only difficult choice to make when entering Keens is where to look first. Is it up, at the 90,000 pipes lining the ceiling? To the glass cases, where the most famous churchwardens—15-inch pipes—smoked by the likes of Babe Ruth and General MacArthur are stored? In the bar, are you mesmerized by the Miss Keen painting (a nude, lounging on her bear rug) right away, or are you too distracted by the Upcoming-York-ad-men-in-the-'50s vibe? This steakhouse, open since 1883, delivers something new to look at every time you go. Keens was originally called a chop house, in recognition of its famous mutton chop, and although that is good and musty and intense, most people are ordering steak. There’s the porterhouse for two or three, the chateaubriand, and the filet mignon—which is actually fabulous here. You want the béarnaise or au poivre sauce on the side, and the creamed spinach, which is less a vegetable than it is dessert. There's also the matter of the burger, which can be ordered up to the dining room from the more casual bar menu. —Alex Van Buren.

1271 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown Manhattan.

Recent findings suggest that from the moment you walk into Cuerno, there's a sense of importance—the crowd, in suits and slicked back hair, is well-dressed; the dining room is always bustling and full, necks turning to see who else has walked in; and tableside preparations are happening left and right. This is Northern Mexican meat at its finest, in a space that feels true to that spirit—substantial leather booths, a colorful tile mural of a skeleton riding a bull—and with a menu that won't let you down. There are expected starters, like fresh guac and queso fundido, but also a chicarrón de pulpo bursting with flavor, and a charcoal-roasted cauliflower complemented by truffle and habanero. The main event, of course, are the steaks, like the decadent Taco Taquero with perfect skirt steak, and fire-roasted bone marrow scooped onto each tortilla tableside, or the Norteño-style arrachera served with chiltepin butter and avocado salsa.

Portions are generous, so come in a group of four people minimum to actually try different sections of the menu. And though most steakhouses focus on wine (and the wine list is good here), I like the chance to pair smoky mezcal and tequila cocktails with the heavier food. —Megan Spurrell.

355 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg, Brooklyn.

Not just in Williamsburg, not just in New York City, but truly one of the coziest, best-value steakhouses I’ve ever been to, St. Anselm manages a rare balance: laid-back yet elevated, intimate without trying too hard, and consistently delicious. The space feels like a hidden tavern—dark wood, low light, and just enough buzz and energy to make it feel like a special night out. The Butcher’s Steak is the standout—charred to perfection, tender and juicy inside, and ideal for sharing (for two) alongside fingerling potatoes and long green beans. Go for a group lunch or, better yet, settle in after dark when the candles are lit and the place feels like a warm, secret pocket of the city. Ask your server—or better yet, belly up to the bar—and you’ll get a wine recommendation that pairs not just with the food, but with your mood. —Jessica Chapel.

513 E 6th Street, East Village, Manhattan.

Industry observers note that buenos Aires earns major points for nostalgia: The tiny dining room is adorned in hanging soccer jerseys, televisions showing live games and commentary, and scarfs and pendants for teams like the Boca Juniors. There are couples on dates, families with kids, and even, in my case, a dude who came in alone and ordered his regular with his headphones in. (Ask about celebrities and they'll bring out an iPad with photos of grinning staff beside countless Latin America soccer players, American actors, and even Matt Damon who apparently hosted two birthday parties here in the early 2000s.) All to say, this isn't the place to bring the corporate account or close the deal, but it is the place to roll up your sleeves and tuck into a massive skirt steak, expertly cooked, and served no-frills—just a great piece of meat on a plate. Do save room for the empanadas (carne cortada a cuchillo, of course); on my next visit, I'm planning to order the sweetbreads as well. —M.S.

Glam, glam, glam with a capital G. Golden Steer's Fresh York iteration—the original is in Vegas, and little of that location's trademark opulence has been sacrificed in adapting the brand for New York. We're not in Midtown either, but in the West Village, and this is a fitting addition to that neighborhood as it increasingly wears its wealth on its sleeve. Entering this crimson bunker is a cinematic experience—long hallways flanked by side quests like the capacious but moody bar. What to get? Sink into your plush booth and go full Sin City: the bloody bull oyster shooter (where a rich beef broth-spiked shot of bloody mary chases the slime), the big ole baked potato, and a Caesar dotingly mixed tableside. Any cut of meat will do. —C.H.

56 Beaver St, Financial District, Manhattan.

The definitive downtown steakhouse is also New York City's oldest. Its home since 1837 is 56 Beaver Street, a dramatic triangular lot at the intersection of Beaver, William, and South William in the Financial District. When I visited on a mid-May evening, the exterior was bedecked in American regalia—they were to film an episode of The Gilded Age there the next day (the new season is presently airing on HBO) depicting the ticker tape parade welcoming the Statue of Liberty to the city. All of this history would be moot were the steakhouse inside not very good, which it is from top to bottom—superlative, doting service in the mural-clad dining room, stiff drinks, perfect cuts of meat. As with every steakhouse, there are a couple of signature items beyond steak that you should consider. Here, it's wedge salad and buttery Lobster Newberg, mentioned to have been invented there. Don't miss either, but steak is still the thing, namely the titular flagship cut—a glistening 18-ounce ribeye that stands alone on the plate, needing no accoutrements. —Charlie Hobbs.

Dinner and a show in Upcoming York City’s midtown sounds fabulous, but in practice usually means settling for a meal that delivers more on convenience than cuisine or atmosphere. Carvesteak, a newish steakhouse on the west side of 48th street, stepped up to all these qualities after I saw The Rocky Horror Show earlier this year. Designed by David Rockwell and the Rockwell Group, it’s moody, mirrored interiors are filled with little nods to the Broadway history it shoulders—including a dramatic velvet curtain that the bartender at the martini bar told me was once part of the set for Andrew Lloyd Webber’s Phantom of the Opera (even if untrue, it certainly looked the part). Speaking of the martini bar, it’s not to be missed: a pocket-sized station to post yourself up at before or after dinner. Food-wise, this is a classic steakhouse menu, but with a little bit of flashiness thanks to the restaurant’s Las Vegas origins (it debuted at Resorts World Las Vegas in 2021): think, prime cuts and aged rib eyes with all the sides and sauces you would expect, but also the option to order a potato and caviar “popsicle.” There’s a pre-theater menu, too, but for the full experience I suggest coming hungry and catching the last call before 10 p.m. —Lale Arikoglu.

  • Four Seasons Yachts has announced a year-long culinary collaboration with Chef Christian Le Squer, executive chef of three-Michelin-starred Le Cinq at Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four Seasons Yachts has announced a year-long culinary collaboration with Chef Christian Le Squer, executive chef of three-Michelin-starred Le Cinq at Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris.

“Sedna is the centerpiece of the culinary program aboard the Four Seasons I, bringing together exceptional talent and a shared passion for creating memorable dining experiences,” stated Ben Trodd, CEO, Marc-Henry Cruise Holdings Ltd., Joint Owner and Operator of Four Seasons Yachts.

“Four Seasons has built an extraordinary culinary community around the world, and I am proud that Le Cinq is part of it,” said Chef Le Squer.

“Bringing this collaboration the Four Seasons I is an exciting evolution, rooted in the same fundamentals that guide us at Le Cinq: a respect for ingredients, a passion for cooking and the pleasure of welcoming guests to the table.

“At Sedna, the menu will draw inspiration from the seasons and the places the Yacht visits, while remaining true to the French cooking that is so close to my heart,” added Chef Le Squer.

Throughout 2027, Chef Le Squer will serve as a culinary ambassador for Sedna, the signature fine-dining restaurant aboard the Four Seasons I, where guests will experience his distinctive interpretation of French gastronomy through a signature tasting menu and an à la carte selection of French gastronomic specialties.

The company remarked in a press release that Chef Le Squer will join two featured Chef-in-Residence voyages, one in the Caribbean in February and another in the Greek Isles in September.

According to the company, the collaboration brings a new dimension to Sedna, connecting Chef Le Squer’s French culinary perspective with the destinations visited by the Four Seasons I.

Extending beyond the menu, Chef Le Squer will help shape Sedna’s culinary direction and guide the continued development of its Chef-in-Residence program.

The press release noted that Sedna’s chefs will train alongside Chef Le Squer and his team at Le Cinq.

Chef Le Squer led the kitchen at Pavillon Ledoyen before joining Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris, as executive chef in 2014.

Chef Christian Le Squer will be featured as Chef-in-Residence on “Lesser Antilles featuring Guadeloupe & Anguilla” (February 21–28, 2027) and “Greek Isles featuring Mykonos & Göcek” (September 12–19, 2027).

Tech Report: The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm.

Sources indicate that bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga highlights in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing claims, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase.

According to recent reports, and there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Major Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

Recent findings suggest that A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next substantial adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

Sources indicate that A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

In a recent development, while it would be a dream to get to every latest hotel within days of opening to be among the first to experience special properties around the world, the reality is, that’s not always possible. When it is, though, you can bet we jump on the opportunity. Especially when it’s a flagship new points hotel.

Sources indicate that that’s how I ended up staying at the gorgeous fresh Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur within a week of its opening on Oct. 30, 2026. To be clear, I understood that not all the hotel’s restaurants would be open, nor would its spa, so this is not a full review, rather a first glimpse at what’s sure to be a favorite Hilton points redemption option soon.

Although it’s the Malaysian capital’s newest hotel, the Waldorf Astoria actually occupies the site of the storied former Hotel Istana in the heart of city’s Golden Triangle district — so called because it is the capital’s main financial and shopping district, with luxury megamalls galore — which means it’s centrally located, but tucked onto a quiet stretch of Jalan Raja Chulan.

Because of that, the hotel feels secluded and quiet, but plugged into the rest of the city, and easily accessible to most of the activities international visitors are likely to seek out while in town.

The hotel feels like a destination unto itself, too, though, thanks to its palatial suites (no mere rooms here) and an impressive slate of bars and restaurants, including outposts from celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten and Bangkok-based Garima Arora. The hotel will also be home to Malaysia’s first and only La Prairie spa, and the outdoor pool is the perfect place to while away a tropical afternoon.

Here’s what else you should strategy to do during your stay at the new Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur.

During my stay, only a fraction of the accommodations were ready for guests, but the hotel should be at full strength soon. There are no rooms here, just suites, which start at an impressive 80 square meters (861 square feet).

Deboss Collective is behind the decor, and sought inspiration from traditional Malay construction and crafts, incorporating lots of natural stone and timber, woven textiles and wooden furnishings that feel like contemporary urban updates to what you might find in a traditional rumah kampung, or village house.

Industry observers note that to wit, there are huge windows overlooking the hotel grounds and the city skyline, letting in plenty of natural light. The carpet patterns and hardwood are meant to evoke traditional Malaysian marquetry while colorful accent walls call to mind vibrant Peranakan shophouses you can still find in parts of the city.

My suite’s footprint was enormous, with a huge, welcoming living area that included a 65-inch flatscreen television, a breakfast table which could double as a workdesk thanks to a panel of plugs, a rounded sofa and armchair and a low-slung wooden chair that blended colonial and midcentury influences.

Recent findings suggest that in the separate bedroom, a king-size bed was dressed with crisp white sheets embroidered with a “WA,” just in case you forgot where you were. To either side were walls with a terete theme hearkening to the bamboo stalks that grow in gardens around the city. Another 55-inch flatscreen hung on the wall in there.

The bathroom was mostly white marble, including geometric floor tiling, but the countertops were a handsome darker hue. Anchoring the entire space was an elliptical standalone tub with a scalloped shell, while a water closet and separate walk-in shower stood close by. To lend a sense of place, the bath products are from Jo Malone’s Jo Loves line and scented with citrusy-fresh pomelo, which is a staple in Malaysian cuisine.

Considering this was a standard category room, it felt positively palatial, with a huge amount of real estate that provided a variety of distinct spaces to enjoy within the suite at different times.

The Waldorf Astoria isn’t the biggest hotel in town, but it fields an outsize roster of restaurants that should be a draw for guests and Kuala Lumpur locals alike.

You can’t call your hotel a Waldorf Astoria if it doesn’t have a version of Peacock Alley, the famous lobby lounge from the Newly introduced York City original. The one here sits smack dab at the hotel entrance and has soaring ceilings, sculptural marble columns, dramatic overhead chandeliers and a variety of seating vignettes that feel homey yet upscale.

The all-day menu offers items like chicken skewers with lemongrass and coriander ($10.50), a Waldorf salad ($14.50), a smash burger ($22) and Malaysian nasi goreng ($17) among other options.

Recent findings suggest that named after the previous hotel to occupy this spot, Istana is the hotel’s all-day dining restaurant and is adjacent to the lobby. Breakfast includes an extensive buffet and both Western and Asian dishes. For lunch and dinner, you’ll find specialties like spiced Borneo chicken wings with a honey glaze ($10.50), chargrilled red snapper with wild ginger chili sambal ($23.75) and fresh fiddlehead ferns from the Cameron Highlands sauteed in coconut milk with tongue-torching bird’s eye chili ($8.75).

If you’re up for it, the durian dessert with coconut cream and a palm sugar compote and served with toasted buttery buns is a rich way to end the evening ($12).

This is Vongerichten’s farm-to-table concept, so you’ll find a menu focused on seasonal fruits and vegetables. The signature eggplant dip is smoky and smooth with tangy coconut yogurt and tomato chutney served with fluffy pita ($9.75). There are also tartines like a king crab crostini with tart lemon aioli and dill ($16.50), various pizzas and pastas, and an array of plant-based dishes including pistachio-crusted broccoli with hazelnut vinaigrette ($14.50).

At the entrance to ABC Kitchens KL, there is a bright, casual area with a cocktail bar and small plates.

Jean-Georges Vongerichten has a longstanding relationship with the Waldorf Astoria brand, so it should be no surprise that the signature restaurant here is a French-Malaysian fine-dining fusion restaurant courtesy of the chef. It is only open for dinner Tuesday-Saturday. I did not have the opportunity to dine here, but the menu features an entire caviar section, starters like diver scallops with caramelized cauliflower and caper-raisin emulsion ($29.50) and spice-charred duck breast with roasted cabbage and chili-lime broth ($39.50).

It was not yet open during my stay, but Yaari will be the hotel’s sophisticated Indian restaurant and will only be open for dinner from Wednesday-Sunday. The chef is Garima Arora, whose Bangkok restaurant, Gaa, holds two Michelin stars.

It has been revealed that located on the fourth floor, Coda feels like a swanky hideaway for those in the know. Glossy dark stone surfaces and emerald-green velvet chairs and banquettes give the space a swanky vibe, as does the menu of libations inspired by various vinyl albums, one of which will likely be spinning on the record player during your visit.

Even the classics get a Malaysian twist, like an old fashioned crafted with jerky-like beef bak kwa-washed Michter’s bourbon, cardamom, clove and cascara distillate and mandarin-infused jaggery for a sweet finish ($20.50).

Industry observers note that the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is an exciting fresh points option in the Malaysian capital, and one with plenty of award availability. While 100,000 points is a lot to pay, considering the sheer size of the suites here and the relatively high (for Kuala Lumpur) price point, it might be well worth it. Once the hotel’s restaurants and spa are all open and operational, this should become one of the city’s most popular luxury hotels.

#144. Industry News: Angus Crichton Promoted to Head of Global Product at Scenic

Industry News: Angus Crichton Promoted to Head of Global Product at Scenic

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Cruiseindustrynews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scenic Group has promoted Angus Crichton to head of global product, bringing his experience across sales, marketing and product development to the leadership of its product teams for Scenic and Emerald Cruises & Tours.
  • Now based at the Group’s office in Zug, Switzerland, he will lead product development across luxury river cruising, yacht cruising and escorted land journeys, strengthening the connection between itinerary design and the guest experience.
  • “As the only organization to design, build, own and operate our ships, we have a truly unique ability to innovate across every aspect of the guest experience, from the luxury spaces on board to the destinations we visit and the journeys we create,” said Sture Myrmell, chief operating officer, Scenic Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scenic Group has promoted Angus Crichton to head of global product, bringing his experience across sales, marketing and product development to the leadership of its product teams for Scenic and Emerald Cruises & Tours.

Now based at the Group’s office in Zug, Switzerland, he will lead product development across luxury river cruising, yacht cruising and escorted land journeys, strengthening the connection between itinerary design and the guest experience.

“As the only organization to design, build, own and operate our ships, we have a truly unique ability to innovate across every aspect of the guest experience, from the luxury spaces on board to the destinations we visit and the journeys we create,” said Sture Myrmell, chief operating officer, Scenic Group.

“That same philosophy connects our ocean, river and land journeys, giving Scenic and Emerald Cruises & Tours guests the confidence to explore in different ways while enjoying a seamless experience with the brands they know and trust. Angus’s deep understanding of our business makes him ideally placed to bring these strengths together as we expand our global portfolio.”.

Crichton previously led marketing, sales and product for Emerald in Australia and Newly introduced Zealand, alongside responsibility for the land product division across Scenic and Emerald.

“Having been part of Scenic Group’s evolution over more than 26 years, I’m excited to help drive its next chapter. Bringing product development and our commercial teams closer together will help us deliver exceptional journeys for our guests and give our travel partners compelling experiences to sell,” noted Crichton.

The appointment comes as Scenic Group progresses what it indicates is its most significant expansion program in decades, with eight upcoming ships planned for 2027 and 2028 and further announcements to come across its luxury river and yacht fleets.

River fleet additions include the Emerald Lumi on France’s Seine River. The ship recently touched water for the first time.

Scenic is also planning expansion to India’s Hooghly River in 2027, with a further ship planned for India’s Brahmaputra River in 2028.

The Scenic Spirit II and Scenic Spirit III are set to debut on the Mekong River from 2028.
